en: May that Gaṇapati grant you auspiciousness—he upon whose cheeks and cheeks-like temples a swarm of graceful bees, intent on drinking, remains silent at every drop of honey-dew trickling down; and who, by his humming, dispels the suspicion that they might be new sapphires. (Rmañj 1.1)

May that Śrī Śāradā, who becomes the blue water-lily (*indīvarī*) for the two lotus-feet of those deities led by Purandara as they perform prostration with the tips of their beautiful crowns, grant the crossing to the further shore of existence (*bhava*).

O Lord! Salutations to You—the auspicious one who bestows the qualities of detachment upon those whose limbs are smeared with ashes, the impeller, the one whose crest is adorned by the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of Smara, the embodiment of Śakti, the Sovereign, the ocean of compassion, the giver of refuge, the treasury of knowledge, the one beyond attributes, the chief of Sūtas, the husband of Girijā, the bearer of the moon, the deity of auspiciousness. The son of Śrī Vaidyanātha, well-guided and of virtuous character, whose name is renowned as Śrī Śālinātha—
Having thus examined various compositions according to the prescribed method, this *Rasamañjarī* is commenced by that virtuous author.
This *Rasamañjarī*, which constantly captivates the hearts of swarms of bees seeking true honey and is filled with manifold aesthetic flavors, is now composed. 1.4.
When inhaled, it removes all diseases of men; when bound, it truly bestows the power of moving through the air with speed.
This seed of Śambhu, worshipped by all the lords of gods and sages—this quicksilver, this pārada—is victorious over the ocean of worldly existence.
Just as fire consumes a great heap of dry fuel,
so does this Sūtra burn away the diseases arising from the three humors.

I bow to the Lord of Mercury (Raseśvara), who, though his splendor cannot even be endured by the masses of light from the moon-crested Lord Śiva, bestows freedom from old age and death and grants the wish-fulfilling tree.
That physician who does not know the mass of compassion, which consists of the essence of Rasā, Hari,
and Hara, performs medical treatment in vain and shall become an object of ridicule.
The action performed by one of deluded mind without service to the guru indeed becomes fruitless, like wealth obtained in a dream. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 1.9)
Those who desire to acquire knowledge through theft, deception, force, and the like—
none of their jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, or other such means will ever succeed.
Accomplished in mantra, a great hero, immovable and devoted to Śiva;
always steadfast, a devotee of the Goddess, and intent upon the sacrifice to the deity.
One who knows the true meaning of all treatises and is skilled in the work of alchemy—
one endowed with these characteristics shall be a master of the science of mercury.
The disciple is devoted to his own guru, truthful in speech, firm in his vows,
free from laziness, knowledgeable in his own duty, and intent upon the propitiation of the Goddess.
(The names of mercury: Śivabīja, Sūtarāja, Pārada, Rasendraka— these are the names of mercury, as well as others, O Śivā, such as these.

That which is deep blue within and brilliant without, or possessing a radiance like the midday sun, is auspicious; likewise, that which is smoky or pure white is praised. However, a variegated [color] should not be employed for the accomplishment of alchemical operations.
When the mercury is freed from its defects, it then removes the pain of death;
it is indeed nectar itself, whereas mercury possessed of defects is poison.
(The defects of mercury: Lead, tin, fiery volatility, unendurability, poison, and mountain-dirt—these impurities are to be known as the defects residing in mercury. (Rmañj 1.17)
These [poisons] produce, in succession, for human beings: stupor, leprosy, great burning fever, loss of virility, fainting, death, eruptions, and a multitude of diseases. (Rmañj 1.18)
(Refining Mercury) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the purification of mercury (*pārada*). One hundred *palas* of mercury should be taken under an auspicious constellation. *Rmañj_1.19*
Fifty, twenty-five, ten, five,
or even just one *pala* less than the full measure must not be used for this supreme refinement of mercury.
(1) Purification of Mercury: Three *palas* of mercury, having been rubbed for three days with a decoction of *citraka*, mustard seeds, *kumārī*, and *kanyā-bṛhatī*,
are freed from the defects of the five impurities and so forth.
(2) For the purification of mercury:
one should grind mercury with a sixteenth part of the powder of brick and *rajanī* in a mortar for one day using the juice extracted from *jambīra* fruits.
(General purification of defects): One should wash the mercury with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*); it thereby abandons the defect of lead.
With the powder of *viśālā* and *aṅkola*, it abandons the defect of tin. *Rmañj_1.23*
The *rājavṛkṣa* tree destroys impurity; fire destroys fire;
the black datura (*kṛṣṇadhattūra*) destroys restlessness; and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) destroy poison. (Rmañj 1.24)
The three pungents (kaṭutraya) destroy mountain-like [diseases], while the three-pronged thorn (trikaṇṭaka) destroys intolerance;
for each respective humor (doṣa), one pala of these should be taken with mercury (sūta) and sour gruel (kāñjika).
Completely freed from all defects and divested of the seven coverings, this purified mercury is born; one should employ it in all ritual actions.
(2) [The Purification of Mercury]: Having placed mercury filtered through a fine cloth into a mortar, one should grind it;
then, having taken it out, the wise man should wash it in an earthen vessel with *āranāla*.
Having added one-tenth part of sulfur to the mercury,
one should grind it for one watch (yāma) with the juice of jambīra fruits, and then subject it to sublimation in a *pātanayantra*.
It should be rubbed again and poured again seven times for the sake of purification;
this is the procedure for the rubbing in a heated mortar for every type of mercury.
(Taptakhalva):
One should place a triad of goat dung, husks, and fire within a pit in the ground;
the mortar situated upon that is known as the *taptakhalva*. (Ramañjari 1.30)
(On the purification of mercury):
One should grind mercury for one day with the powders of *kumārī* and turmeric;
by sublimating it in a *pātanāyantra*, the mercury becomes perfectly pure.
(Refining Mercury): One should grind mercury with the juices of *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *devadāru*, and *kākatuṇḍī*, as well as *jayā*;
then, having added the juice of *karkoṭī*, *musalī*, and *kanyā*, one should thoroughly rub it.
One should then rub it for one day and employ it once purified. (This is the purification of mercury. Alternatively, one may extract mercury from cinnabar; that is now described. Rmañj 1.33.

Cinnabar rubbed for a day with the juice of *jambīra* and lime (*nimbū*) should be processed by means of an upward-ascension apparatus (*ūrdhvapātanayantra*); thus the pure essence (*rasa*) is obtained.
Freed from its "shields" such as nāgavaṅga and others during the process of alchemical work,
this mercury performs all operations even without the eightfold ritual procedure.

This wonderful and supreme method for purifying mercury, which is the consensus of all perfected adepts, bestows abundant accomplishments through even a few ritual procedures; indeed, it is highly praised for the transmutation of bodies and metals.
Indeed, for one who consumes the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) devoid of purification (saṃskāra), it causes affliction;
it brings about the destruction of the body, various types of leprosy, and generates painful diseases for men. (Rmañj 1.37)
Rmañj 2:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme digestion of mercury (rasajāraṇa).
Furthermore, one who causes the death of mercury that is undigested or seedless (abīja) [is at fault]. Rmañj_2.1.
O Maheśvarī, that evil-doer is a slayer of Brahmins and a traitor to me;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause the mercury to die once it has been processed.

Having poured water into an earthen vessel and placed a small cup upon it, one should set down within it a powder provided with a surrounding rim. (The sublimation of mercury by means of *bali*). Rmañj_2.3.
Having added the liquid, one should sprinkle the powder of sulphur on top of it;
then, having added an equal portion, one should cover it with a shallow dish.
Then the best of physicians should perform the very light ash-seal (bhasmamudrā) and properly apply a sealed enclosure (puṭa) using four forest stones.
O Goddess, having thus repeatedly applied fragrance again and again, the best of physicians should properly perform the sixfold digestion of the elixir.

(On the digestion of mercury and gold: Mercury, ground for three nights with salt, *śigru*, *tuttha*, *rājika* mustard, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), then its body having been steamed, consumes all metals, beginning with the foremost, gold. (Rmañj 2.7)
(Alchemical processing of mercury): Alternatively, smeared with *biḍa* salt and peacock bile,
the king of elixirs (*rasarāja*) may move through gold at will in a heated mortar.
O Goddess, powdered conch-shell that has been burnt and saturated with the milk of the sun (ravikṣīra),
when subjected to a hundred *puṭa* cycles, is known by the wise as the excellent method for *jāraṇa*.
One should digest gold, mica, and all metals as desired;
by various methods, the wise one should digest mercury starting from the sixty-fourth part,
and [subsequently] digest gold using the thirty-second or sixteenth part.
(Regarding the killing of mercury: Two palas of purified mercury and half that amount of purified sulfur should be ground together continuously for one day with the juice of *kanyā* [goddess plant].
Having sealed it in that earth-based apparatus, one should perform the *puṭa* roasting for one day to kill the mercury (*rasamāraṇa*).
The mercury should be thoroughly rubbed with the juice of the *bhujaṅgavallī* plant. (Rasamāraṇa 2) *Rmañj* 2.12.

The ash, placed within a crucible made of earth from the root of the *karkoṭī* plant and subjected to the "elephant" (*gaja*) type of *puṭa* heating, becomes a "conveyor of application" (*yogavāhin*); one should employ it in all ritual actions.
The mercury should be rubbed for three days with the juice of the roots of white *Aṅkola*; then,
having been subjected to a *puṭa* in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the mercury attains the state of ash.
If one should eat five *raktikās* daily with honey and clarified butter, what man on earth is able to describe its virtues? (Rmañj 2.15)
(1) For the preparation of *rasasindūra*: take one *pala* of purified mercury and an equal amount of *sugandhaka*;
having duly prepared a collyrium (*kajjalī*) from these with the juice of *nyagrodha* sprouts, [proceed as follows].
Having performed the threefold meditation, one should place [the vessel] inside a crucible;
having fashioned the *kavacī* instrument, one should fill it with sand.
Rasa-sindūra is produced, resembling the hue of the young rising sun; through specific adjuncts (anupāna), it produces various medicinal qualities. (Ramañjari 2.18)
Mercury equal in weight to sulphur, rubbed with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and cooked in a *vālukāyantra*, produces red ash. (Rasa-sindūra II)

Take half a part of mercury (*sūtārddha*) and purified sulfur (*gandhaka*), along with the essence (*sattva*) extracted from *mākṣika* ore; having ground these together with an equal amount of sulfur for one day using the juice of *nirguṇḍī*, [one obtains] *rasasindūra*.

One should place it in a sand-bath apparatus (*vālukāyantra*) within a glass flask (*kācakūpyā*) and cook it; or else, having placed it inside a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should cook it in a sand-bath apparatus for a day.
When cooked, it becomes an ash resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree (*rasasindūra*).
Having prepared mercury and sulfur in equal parts, [one should proceed as follows]. (Rasa-sindūra, 2.22)
Having ground together navasāra, dhūmasāra, and sphaṭikī for the duration of one watch (yāma) with the juice of nimbu, one should cook them in a glass vessel.
Having placed a stone pellet inside the mouth, one should seal it with a coating;
then, having dried it separately with seven layers of clay-cloth, one should wrap it.
The wise physician should place a small jar inside a clay pot that has a hole in it, and fill it with sand up to the neck. (Rmañj 2.25)
Having placed the fire on the hearth and kindled it slowly, with moderate intensity,
one should remove it when it has become cool to the touch, after twelve watches (yāmas) have passed.
Having opened the vessel again, one should discard the sulphur that has moved upward;
the mercury-cinnabar remaining at the bottom should be employed in all ritual procedures.
Take equal parts of mercury vermilion (*rasasindūra*), sulfur, [the substance denoted by the symbol *au1*], and purified mercury;
grind them together for one watch (*yāma*) in a mortar and place the mixture in a glass flask. (Ramañjari 2.28)

Having sealed it for twelve *yāmas*, one should cook it in a sand-bath (*vālukāyantra*). Once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body, one should break [the vessel]; that which remains adhered to the upper part should be discarded, while the mercury (*sūta*) situated at the bottom, now deceased, should be employed in all formulations.
Take two parts of mercury (*rasa*), three parts of sulfur (*gandha*), and one part of *pavanāsana* (mercurial calamine);
having thoroughly ground all these together in a fine vessel, one should place that collyrium (*kajjalī*) in a glass container. (Rasa-sindūra, 2.30)

Having wrapped it in clay-soaked rags and having made fine powder of chalk by hand, one should cook it for three days with a gradual fire; thereafter, it shall be situated within a sand-vessel (*vālukāyantra*).
The ash of the Lord’s son, as red as the bandhūka flower, should be applied for all diseases;
when used with its own appropriate adjuncts and through the practice of *vallaka*, it destroys both death and old age.

Having placed mercury and sulphur— equal in quantity, finely powdered, and arranged with the mercury below and the sulphur above— inside a sealed crucible (*pakvamūṣā*), one should again add the juice of *kākamācī*.
Having sealed the crucible with four times as much liquid as the two [ingredients],
one should cook it in a *vālukāyantra* for a day with a fire gradually increased in intensity. A reddish ash is produced, which should be employed in all formulations.
The mercury should be carefully sweated with the group of herbs beginning with *aśvagandhā*;
then, a skilled physician should grind it together with an equal amount of sulfur. (Rasasindūra) Rmañj 2.35.
One should cook it until *rasasindūra* is produced, which resembles the color of dawn;
for it is the best of all mercury-based elixirs, bestowing nourishment, desire, and strength. (Ramañjari 2.36)
This alone is sufficient to increase one's lifespan;
nothing else is capable of doing so, as proclaimed by the sages even without the king of gold.
One should grind together mercury, borax, honey, lac, wool, and *guñjā* seeds,
or otherwise heat the mercury again after having rubbed it for one day with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
When heated, it turns to ash and becomes pure like camphor (*rasakarpūra*).
Equal parts of *khaṭī*, *iṣṭikā*, red ochre (*gairika*), anthill earth (*valmīkamṛttikā*), and rock salt (*saindhava*) [are used]. (Rmañj 2.39)
Having placed two parts of fragrance and two parts of liquid into the pot, one should arrange rags along each side [of the vessel]. (Rmañj 2.40)
Having burnt [the crucible] and placed it in a *haṇḍikā* vessel, one should cook it for sixteen *praharas*;
then one should take the dead mercury, which is pure and resembles camphor.
Having wrapped it in *kalka* and other substances, one should swallow it in cases of *upadaṃśaka*.

The pure mercury (*sūta*) should be ground many times with *vajrī* water along with salt (*pāṃśu*), *paṭu*, and *pragāḍha*, combined with metallic ores (*dhātu*), and encased in *khaṭī*; this should then be sealed within a crucible (*sampuṭa*).
Having forcefully ignited a fire beneath that salt which stands within [the vessel], one should then gradually take the ash, white as the moon or a kunda flower, situated upon the ashes.
Similarly, this pair of *vallī* plants taken together with cloves, consumed by men in the morning, causes vomiting repeatedly for two watches of the night; cool water should be drunk after it.

This destroys poison for a period of a year—whether six-monthly or monthly—and neutralizes mineral poison, snake venom, and even instantaneous poison produced by the crooked king of beasts (the lion).
(Rasamūrchana) One should grind the mercury with meghanāda, vacā, hiṅgu, and garlic;
once it has become a "disappeared-paste" (naṣṭapiṣṭa), one should wrap that ball externally with hiṅgu. Rmañj 2.44.
Having placed it in a salt-vat for one day over a fierce fire,
one should take it out while it is still hot and wrap it firmly with a cloth.
Having added an equal amount of sulphur above and below, one should cook it over a gentle fire;
when the sulphur is consumed, more should be added six times, in equal portions each time.
When six times its weight of sulfur has been digested [by the mercury], it becomes a disease-destroyer once it has undergone *mūrchana* (solidification).
[Regarding *rasamūrchana*:
One *pala* of pure sulfur [is placed] in an iron or copper vessel. *Rmañj_2.47*
When that has been melted by a mild fire, one should add three palas of purified lead and stir it repeatedly with an iron ladle.
One should apply cow dung and a plantain leaf over that;
thus, this "perfume-binding" should be employed for all diseases. (Rmañj 2.49)
It is "killed" (mārita) for the sake of achieving bodily perfection; it is "fainted" (mūrchita) for the destruction of diseases.
In some cases, mercury-ash (rasabhasma) is used for a specific ailment; in other cases, it is "fainted" for the sake of the body.
One should employ the "bound" (baddha) form using the procedures seen in the scriptures, as both methods serve the purpose.
(The characteristics of bound mercury: It is inexhaustible, light, fusible, radiant, stainless, and heavy;
furthermore, its bursting and returning [to its original state] are the characteristics of bound mercury. (Rmañj 2.51)
(Characteristics of the solidified mercury): When the mercury, having abandoned its intense volatility, appears with the luster of collyrium,
then it should be known by the wise as being thoroughly solidified (*mūrchita*).
(Characteristics of dead mercury):
One should know that to be dead mercury in which moisture, density, mobility, heaviness, and brilliance are not observed. (Rmañj 2.53)
(Regarding *nirbījabaddhapārada*):

Mercury that has been digested with gold in the proportion of one-quarter part, reduced to a paste through the application of sulfur, and then subjected to successive *puṭa* treatments with equal parts of sulfur, is named *nirbīja*; it is the destroyer of all diseases. (Rmañj 2.54)
(Regarding mercury bound with seed): This [mercury],
having been processed together with *abhraka*-essence, gold, copper, iron, and magnetite that have been converted into seed (*bījīkṛta*),
and then further treated with sixfold quantities of powdered sulfur, is "bound with seed" (*sabījabaddha*) and possesses even greater potency.
One should know that mercury is composed of nectar in its taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation;
when constantly consumed, it serves to destroy diseases within the body.
(Kakārāṣṭaka) The kūṣmāṇḍa, the karkaṭī, the kaliṅga, the kāravellaka, the kusumbhika, the karkoṭī, the kadalī, and the kākamācikā. Rmañj 2.57.
One who consumes meat should indeed avoid these eight syllables beginning with *ka*;
for it is beneficial to consume mung beans, water, milk, ghee, and especially *śāli* rice.
One should eat the leaf of *punarnavā*, *meghanāda*, *cillikā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), ginger (*nāgara*), *musta*, and the roots of the lotus. (Rmañj 2.59)

One may enjoy anointing the body with oil, sexual union, bathing as one desires with pleasant water, and consorting with a beloved wife who is endowed with beauty and youth and is well-disposed toward him.
Intellect, wisdom, strength, luster, radiance, and likewise vitality—all these indeed increase for men through the practice of consuming [medicinal] juices. (Rmañj 2.61)
Whichever formulation corresponds to whichever disease, by employing that very same one,
the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) removes the ailments of men, elephants, and horses.
O Beloved, the secondary minerals (uparasas) are sulphur, diamond, vaikrānta, gaganam, talaka, and realgar.
Kharpara, śikhituttha, vimalā, and hemamākṣika; 3.1.
Copper sulfate, magnetite, cowrie shells, collyrium, vermilion, kaṅkuṣṭha, conch-shell, bhūnāga, borax, and bitumen; Rmañj 3.2.
These are declared to be the minor minerals (uparasa); they are to be purified, liquefied, and killed.
First, the origin of sulfur (gandhaka) is described, and then its purification is told. Rmañj 3.3.
Long ago on Śvetadvīpa, while the Goddess was sporting, her menstrual flow was emitted;
furthermore, when she had bathed in the Ocean of Milk, her silken garment was stained with that flow.
That which is washed in that water is known as fragrant sulphur (gandhaka).
Sulphur is said to be of four kinds: red, yellow, white, and black.
The red variety is praised for gold-making; the yellow is excellent for alchemy (rasāyana);
the white is best for applying ointments to wounds and the like; the black, however, is rare to find.
Impure fragrance causes severe skin diseases, fever, dizziness, and bilious ailments;
it destroys one's appearance, happiness, virility, and strength. Therefore, [the ointment] should be applied only when it is thoroughly purified.
(1) Purification of sulfur:
Having poured milk into a vessel containing clarified butter, one should seal its mouth with a cloth;
having placed the sulfur on top of that, one should cover it with a shallow bowl.
Having placed the vessel upon the ground, one should place a light packet above it;
then, with milk, one should employ pure fragrance in the various applications.
(2) Purification of Sulfur:
The knower of reality should purify sulfur in milk using a dolāyantra (swinging apparatus).
By this, it becomes pure, acting as the life-sustaining vitalizer for the minerals. (Rmañj 3.10)
(3) [The Purification of Sulphur]:
One should melt sulphur mixed with clarified butter in a fire using an iron ladle;
once it has become a single mass, one should then cast the sulphur into the midst of milk. Rmañj_3.11 //
By that means the fragrance becomes pure; one should employ it in all formulations.
Once purified, the king of essences (mercury) shall become the remover of old age, death, and disease;
it is excellent for kindling the digestive fire and increases virility.

One should coat a cloth seven times with either the milky sap of the *arka* plant or the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant; then, having ground sulfur with butter, one should smear that [cloth] with it. (Rmañj 3.13)
The wick made from that [substance] should be held by means of bamboo tubes and maintained with its tip facing downwards.
The oil falls into the lower vessel; it should be collected and employed in medicinal formulations.
It is excellent for stimulating the digestive fire and increases virility.
White, yellow, red, and black are the types of diamonds belonging to the twice-born classes and so forth;
one should identify them by their characteristics as male, female, or neuter. (Ratnāvalī 3.16)
Those which are round, filled with seeds, radiant, and very large,
are declared to be male, being devoid of lines and dots.
Those [lines] joined with lines and dots are known as female;
those triangular and elongated like leaves are to be understood as neuter. (Rmañj 3.18)
Among all [practitioners], men are the best as piercers and binders of mercury;
for the sake of attaining the perfection of the body, the *strīvajra* is used, while the *napuṃsaka* serves as the transmuter (*krāmaṇa*).
The Brahmin is declared to be for alchemy (rasāyana), the Kṣatriya for the destruction of diseases;
the one of Vaiśya birth is for debate and the like, and the fourth [the Śūdra] for the stabilization of youth.
A female [seal] should be given to a woman, and likewise a neuter one to a eunuch;
however, among all [genders], the male [seals] are always to be employed as the most powerful.
An unrefined diamond brings about jaundice, pain in the flanks, leprosy, a continuous burning sensation, a host of diseases, and heaviness. (Rm 3.22)
(1) The Purification of Vajra:
The vajra placed within the bulb of a tigress plant and cooked in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) for seven days in a decoction of *kodrava* and *kaulattha* beans becomes pure. Rmañj 3.23.
(Vajra-purification (2)):
One should cook a vajra placed inside a *vyāghrī* tuber, coated with clay, in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*).
Having extracted it after one day and night, one should sprinkle it with horse urine.
Or one may sprinkle it with *vajrī* milk; the thunderbolt will then become stainless.
(Vajramāraṇa 1) One should take the root of three-year-old cotton (*kārpāsa*), grind it,
and then grind it again with the juice of three-year-old *nāgavallī*.
One should cast the vajra into that crucible, seal it, and cook it in a "gajapuṭa" fire;
by performing this seven times, the thunderbolt is certainly killed.
In a bell-metal vessel, one should thoroughly soak a diamond in the urine of a frog; heated twenty-one times, the diamond itself will become dead. (Vajramāraṇa 2) Rmañj_3.27 //
One should sprinkle [the substance] heated twenty-one times with donkey urine; having ground realgar with bedbugs, one should place the vajra within that globule. (Vajramāraṇa 3) Rmañj 3.28.
Blown with horse urine and sprinkled according to the previous procedure, it is reduced to ashes; when consumed, it makes the body like a diamond.
Vajra-ash is truly capable of bestowing longevity, generating happiness, granting strength, and likewise granting beauty; it destroys disease and removes death. (Rmañj 3.30)
Eight-sided, with eight facets, hexagonal, smooth, and heavy;
endowed with pure or mixed colors—this is called vaikrānta. (Rmañj 3.31)
White, red, yellow, blue,
the color of a pigeon, dark, black, and variegated— thus he is indeed eightfold.
(Purification of Vaikrānta):
Vaikrānta is purified like a diamond;
when it is melted in horse urine, that beneficial ash should be employed by the wise in place of diamond.

Vaikrāntaka indeed bestows longevity, binds all [the bodily constituents], is highly aphrodisiac, grants wisdom, uproots the entire collection of diseases, stimulates the digestive fire, possesses qualities equal to those of iron, is full of vigor, and produces physical strength and iron. (Ramañjari 3.34)
(The precipitation of the essence of vaikrānta: One should grind vaikrānta and vajrakanda with vajra-water;
then, having mixed in buffalo butter and honey, it should be formed into a ball.
Having dried it, one should heat the essence until it becomes like an *indragopa* insect;
(*abhraka*) is of four kinds: *pināka*, *dardura*, *nāga*, and *vajra*.
It completely casts off its mass of petals when scorched in the fire, like the Pināka bow.
One should perform the *phūtkāra* like a serpent and the *dardura* like the croaking of a frog;
the fourth is to be known as the "excellent," and one should not undergo any transformation within the fire.
Therefore, one should take vajrābhra (diamond-like mica), which conquers disease, old age, and death;
for impure mica destroys longevity and increases wind and phlegm.
If one smelts [abhraka] that has not been processed, it increases weak digestion and worms;
therefore, pure abhraka should be taken, for it destroys weak digestion and worms. (Rmañj 3.39)

Having bound the mica (*abhra*) mixed with a quarter-part of rice (*śāli*) in a *kambala* cloth, one should place it in water for three nights; once it is moistened, one should grind it firmly. (Rmañj 3.40)
That which has fallen from a woolen blanket, being smooth and free of grit, is called *dhānyābhra* by the wise for the sake of accomplishing the body. (Rmañj 3.41)
(On the preparation of grain-like mica):
One should smelt vajra-mica in fire and then sprinkle it with milk;
having thus made its leaves split apart, one should treat it with the juices of meghanāda and amlavetasa.
The wise one should cultivate that for eight watches and cause that "grain-like mica" (dhānyābhra) to be prepared.
Alternatively, one should place mica that has been smelted in a decoction of *badarī* fruit;
once it has been rubbed with the hand and dried, it excels even *dhānyābhra*.
(Tin ash: One part of grain-tin (*dhānyābhra*) and two parts of borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
Having ground it and sealed it in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), one should cook it with a fierce fire;
once cooled naturally, the powder should be employed for all diseases. (Rmañj 3.45)
(1) For the sublimation of mica:
Firm grain-mica should be ground for as many days as there are suns [twelve] in the milk of the *arka* plant;
one should then wrap it with *arka* leaves and fashion it into the shape of a wheel.
It should be cooked repeatedly seven times in a crucible called the *kuñjara*;
then, likewise, three more *puṭas* should be administered with decoctions of *vaṭa* roots.
Indeed, death is called doubt; one should apply this among all diseases.
(The Killing of Clouds [2]) Having taken *dhānyābhraka* (grain-like mica), one should subject it to three *puṭa* cycles with decoctions of *mustaka*. (Rmañj 3.48)
Likewise, it should be combined separately with the juices of punarnavā and nīra,
as well as with the juices of kāsamarda and nāgavallī, and with the milks of the sun-plant (sūrya).
Having crushed it day after day with decoctions produced from the roots of the *vaṭa* tree,
one should subsequently apply three *puṭas* [of heat], followed by three *puṭas* with the juices of *muśalī*.
One should roast it three times with a decoction of gokṣuraka, three times with the juices of vānarī,
cook it three times with the juices of mocākanda, and three times with kokilākṣaka.
Then one should perform the *puṭa* process with the juices, followed by the *dhenu-puṭa*, and repeatedly with alkaline water,
curd, ghee, honey, and likewise with clear white sugar.
One should give each layer of mica individually; in this way, its death occurs.
The sky [of mercury] becomes a bearer of yoga, removing all diseases.
It destroys the intoxication and pride of women, is praised for those seeking virility,
is aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, increases semen, and brings about progeny.
The three milks, virgin’s water, *gaṅgā* leaf, human urine, banyan sprouts, and goat blood— having thoroughly ground the mica with these; Rmañj 3.55.
When folded a hundred times, the ash becomes like a ruby;
the sky becomes moonless, and the elixir is the purified body.
The form of space, devoid of the moon, produces vigor and a firm body;
it destroys death and the entire multitude of old age and diseases.

(Extracting the essence of mica): Mica that has been infused and powdered should be mixed with sour gruel for one day, and then combined with the juices of plantain and suraṇa, as well as those arising from radish. Rmañj_3.58
Then, having combined this with one-fourth part of ṭaṅkaṇa, along with small fish and the impurities of a buffalo, one should prepare a pill from it.
One should intensely heat the essence with a fierce fire; it will release its radiant luster.
A wise person who has performed purification and cultivates that essence shall attain the stabilization of youth.
(Alchemical Dissolution of Abhraka):
When abhraka is ground with the exudation of *agasti* flowers and placed inside a *sūraṇa* root,
situated in a cow-pen, it becomes as bright as the sky and resembles water.
(General method for precipitating sattva: molasses, lac, oil-cake, and borax; likewise wool, resin, and small fish. Rmañj 3.62.
Having ground all of this together and formed it into a pill with goat’s milk, one should heat it over the embers of a donkey; it will cause all sentient beings to fall down.
Stones, clay, and so forth, as well as all types of metals,
and whatever other things are incurable— what need is there to mention the being of space?
When there is a secondary state in a flavor, one must apply the presence of its corresponding quality;
if you desire to be a knower of flavors, you must increase those qualities.
(Regarding the subduing of the earth-nāga being):
Having immediately taken the earth-nāga, the wise one should cause it to enter a peacock;
or else, having made a brave cock take refuge in its dwelling. *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa* 3.66.
Having taken the feces and urine and discarded the first portion,
one should diligently stir in milk, honey, and clarified butter, and blow upon it for the sake of sentient beings.
They release their essence like copper; by drinking the water consecrated with that mudrā, all mobile poisons without exception are destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (Rmañj 3.68)
(Defects of impure haritāla):
Impure *tāla* destroys longevity and causes phlegm, wind, and urinary disorders; it produces vomiting, eruptions, and contraction of the limbs; therefore, one should purify it. (Rmañj 3.69)
Haritāla (orpiment) becomes pure when it has been steamed in the juice of kūṣmāṇḍa, then in powdered water,
and separately in oil; once reduced to ashes, it causes no harm.
Copper removes diseases such as leprosy and the pains of death;
when thoroughly purified, it bestows luster and vigor, and indeed increases longevity. (Rmañj 3.71)
(The Killing of Haritāla):

One *pala* of pure *tāla* [mineral] should be rubbed with the juice of *kaumāra* [plant] and placed inside a double-layered earthen bowl (*śarāva-sampuṭa*); it should then be cooked for twelve *yāmas*.
Having taken the mineral calamine (tālaka) once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, it becomes "dead" (neutralized);
this calamine undoubtedly removes even flowing leprosy (galatkuṣṭha).
(Refining Realgar): Realgar is purified by being infused seven times with water from the *agasti* leaf,
or else it is purified by the juices of ginger.
Realgar (manaḥśilā) is pungent, unctuous, and bitter; it is supreme for destroying phlegm and scraping away impurities.
It destroys the affliction of possession by spirits, and this auspicious substance relieves cough and asthma.
(Purification of Rasaka):
One should cook rasaka for seven days with human urine and donkey urine using a dolāyantra;
having thus purified it, one should employ it in various applications.
(Refining Tuttha):

A physician should take tuttha equal in measure to human excrement, along with honey and *ṭaṅkaṇa* water; having been subjected to three types of *puṭapāka* firing, it becomes pure and free from vomiting and dizziness. *Rmañj 3.77*
(Tuttha-guṇas: Tutthaka is pungent, alkaline, astringent, clear, and light; it is scraping, fissuring, beneficial for the eyes, and removes itching, worms, and poison. (Rmañj 3.78)
Steeped in the juice of *jambīra* or in the juice of *meṣaśṛṅgī*,
or cooked with the water of *rambhā* for one day, this is for the sake of the purity of the *vimala*.
Take one part of rock salt produced from the Sindhu region and three parts of honey;
having placed these in an iron vessel, one should then stir them with an iron ladle.
One should cook it over a mild fire until it takes on the appearance of vermilion; one should know this as *subhadra-mākṣika* and employ it in all formulations. (Rmañj 3.81)
(Regarding the killing of *mākṣika*):
Having added one-fourth part of sulfur to the *mākṣika*, one should grind it;
then, with the oil of *ūrubūka*, a fine pellet (*cakrikā*) should be prepared.
Having placed it in a pair of earthen saucers, one should roast it with a *gajapuṭa* fire;
the ash of the *mākṣika* will undoubtedly become the color of vermilion.
(The properties of honey:
Honey is bitter and sweet; it cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, consumption, and skin diseases.
It removes phlegm and bile, is strengthening, acts as a vehicle for other substances, and is a rejuvenative elixir.
(Purification of green vitriol):
Green vitriol that has been steamed once with the water of *bhṛṅga* becomes stainless.
(The qualities of kāsīsa):
Kāsīsa is cooling, unctuous, and when heated, it removes eye diseases;
it pacifies bile and epilepsy, and like mercury, it produces beneficial qualities.

One should place salts and alkalis along with *kāntapāṣāṇa* into the juice of *śobhāñjana*, and first let it soak for half a day combined with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*). (Rmañj 3.87)
The wise one should cook it for a day in a dolikāyantra with those fluids;
once the kāntapāṣāṇa is purified, one should perform the alchemical operation (rasakarma).
(Varāṭikās):
Varāṭikās are yellowish in luster, knotted on the back, and long and oval;
those weighing one and a half niṣkas are excellent, while those weighing one niṣka are middling.
Those weighing three-quarters of a niṣka are proclaimed as the lowest;
they are designated by the physicians of mercury as "mobile" (cara) and "immobile" (acara).
(Purification of cowries):
Cowries, having been steamed in sour gruel for one watch (three hours), attain purification.
(The qualities of cowries).
It cures colic caused by morbid transformation and other ailments, and it destroys disorders of the digestive tract and consumption.
Pungent and hot, it stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and removes wind and phlegm;
it is said to be used for the digestion of mercury and is recommended among the substances known as *viḍa*.
(Refining cinnabar): Cinnabar, having been processed with ewe’s milk and the group of sour substances seven times with great care, certainly attains purity. (Rmañj 3.93)
(The qualities of cinnabar:

Cinnabar is divine, bitter and hot, produced from mercury and sulfur; it removes urinary disorders and skin diseases, promotes relish for food, is strengthening, and stimulates the intellect and the digestive fire. (Ramañjari 3.94)
(Refining Śilājatu): Śilājatu ground with cow’s milk, triphalā, and the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, and kept for one day in an iron vessel, undoubtedly attains purification. (Rmañj 3.95)
(On the Qualities of Śilājatu):
Śilājatu is bitter, pungent, and hot; it is a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
It destroys consumption, wasting, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids, and it conquers the pains of the bladder. *Ramañjuśrī-mūlakalpa* 3.96.
Sauvīra, ṭaṅkaṇa, conch shell, kaṅkuṣṭha, and likewise gairika—
these should be purified like cowries and become free from defects.
(Purification of Jewels):
A ruby is purified by sour gruel, likewise a pearl by *jayantī*;
coral by the group of alkaline substances, and emerald by cow’s milk.
One should stabilize the topaz with *kulattha* bean decoctions mixed with *taṇḍulīya* water,
and the diamond and sapphire with indigo juice.
Gomedaka is [purified] with rocanā, and vaidūrya with the waters of triphalā;
[these are to be used] together with realgar, sulphur, and yellow orpiment ground with the juice of lakucha.
(The Purification of Gems)
Indeed, other gems besides the diamond are destroyed by eight layers [of fire].
(The qualities of jewels: Pearl, coral, diamond, sapphire, lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth.
The maṇi-jewel is hard, cool, astringent, sweet, and scraping; by wearing it, it is beneficial for the eyes and removes evil, misfortune, and poison. (Rmañj 3.102)
O Mañjuśrī, the eighteen kinds of poisons that are proclaimed to be bulb-born should be known.
Kālakūṭa, Mayūra, Binduka, and likewise Saktuka.
Vāluka, vatsanābha, śaṅkhanābha, sumaṅgala, śṛṅgī,
markaṭaka, musta, kardama, puṣkara, and śikhī.
The poison called hālāhala is turmeric-colored, green, circular, dense, dry, hard, and has a luster like that of crushed collyrium. (Appearance of Poisons) Rmañj 4.3.
The great poison Kālakūṭa is described as having the appearance of a bulb;
that which resembles a peacock is called Mayūra, and Binduka is known by its bindu-like form.
The *citram* is like the root of a blue lotus; the *śaktukam* is like a grain of millet; the *vālukam* has the appearance of sand; and the *vatsanābham* is pale white.
That which resembles a conch-navel, has the color of a conch, is of a brilliant white hue, and is highly auspicious;
that which is dense, heavy, compact, and shaped like a horn is called *śṛṅgika*.
Markaṭa has the appearance of a monkey; mustaka has the form of a musta root;
kardama has the appearance of mud; and kardama is white and yellow.
Puṣkara is lotus-shaped; Śikhi has the luster of a peacock’s crest;
Hāridraka has the appearance of turmeric; and Harita is known as green.
The wheel should be circular in shape and the color of Halāhala poison, which is blue;
there, the Brāhmaṇa is white and the Kṣatriya is red in color.
The Vaiśya has a yellow luster, while the Śūdra is blackish and considered censurable.
A Brāhmaṇa [image] is given for diseases, a Kṣatriya for cases of poison ingestion,
a Vaiśya for all types of illnesses, and a Śūdra for one bitten by a snake.
When that poison is ground together with an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), it is said to be "dead. One should employ it in all diseases, for it indeed causes no adverse reaction. (Rmañj 4.11)
Having made the poisonous portions as large as grains of rice and placed them in a vessel,
one should then add cow’s urine, fresh every single day. (Rmañj 4.12)
Then, having placed it in intense sunlight, one should dry it for more than three days; thereafter, one should employ that poison in medicinal applications according to the prescribed dosage.
The consumption of poison is said to bring about death; now, therefore, I shall explain its ritual service (*sevā*).
One should cause [the rite] to be performed during autumn, summer, spring, and the rainy season;
during the four-month period, it removes diseases, even those such as leprosy and skin-eruptions.
On the first day, the dose is the size of a mustard seed; on the second, two mustard seeds;
and likewise on the third, fourth, and fifth days.
In the sixth and seventh [stages], one should increase them by successive increments;
the first group of seven should consist of the size of seven mustard seeds.
Likewise, in the second week, there is a gradual decrease;
in the third week, the poison is administered in increasing doses by the measure of a barley grain.
It should be administered during periods of increase or decrease, as well as on the fourth and seventh days;
one who is healthy should swallow a dose the size of a barley grain, while one suffering from leprosy should take a dose the size of a *guñjā* berry.
Poison should not be given to one who is eighty years of age, nor to one whose wealth has been exhausted; if it were given, it would cause harm.

One should administer [this] in all diseases to one who eats only what is beneficial and consumes the "eater of the dead" (mṛtāśin); furthermore, a person devoted to elixirs (rasāyana) should employ a diet of milk.
For celibacy is paramount; one should practice it as if it were poison.
Having become healthy-minded regarding what is wholesome, success will then follow without a doubt.
When a mortal, through negligence, consumes poison in an excessive dose, then eight stages of its effect arise; of this there is no doubt.
In the first stage there is agitation; in the second, trembling occurs;
in the third, there is a terrible burning sensation; and in the fourth, one falls to the ground.
In the fifth stage, there is frothing at the mouth; in the sixth, there is loss of sensory function;
in the seventh stage, there is numbness; and in the eighth, death occurs.
Having recognized the forces of poison, one should destroy them by means of mantras and tantras;
this was spoken from the mouth of Sadāśiva for the benefit of practitioners.
For the purpose of destroying all poisons, this supreme mantra is proclaimed.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Ghoṇeya! Hara, hara! Dara, dara! Para, para! Tara, tara! Vara, vara! Vadha, vadha! Vaḥ, vaḥ! Laḥ, laḥ! Raṃ, raṃ! Lāṃ, lāṃ, lāṃ! Haralāṃ! Hara, hara! Bhava! Sara! Rāṃ, rāṃ! Kṣīṃ, kṣīṃ! Hīṃ, hīṃ! O Blessed Lady Śrīghoṇeya! Saṃ, saṃ, saṃ! Vara, vara! Rasaḥ! Dha! Vara, vara! Khaṇḍa!
And O form, hrīṃ, excellent bird, speak of security for humanity; O enemy of Śeṣa, O enemy of Śeṣa, ṣaṣaḥ svāhā!
By the mere recollection of this vidyā, the *guṭhaka* and other such afflictions are destroyed.
One should sprinkle water empowered by seven recitations upon that which is impelled by time. (Rmañj 4.29)
One should rise up with fervor and bind the topknot;
if one sounds a conch or a drum consecrated by the three mantras, [the rite is successful].
Even in another country or within one's own body, it renders poison harmless in an instant.
Whenever the mantra-practitioner, having seen [the venom], recites the mantra even once,
it becomes poison-free upon being seen— even if it be the poisons of hundreds of Māras.
By drinking cow’s ghee, the *vandhyakarkoṭī* removes various poisons;
likewise, the *triśūlikā* and the *surabhijihvā* pacify all defects caused by poison.
Poison is neutralized by mere rubbing with *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt when one is satisfied;
however, if one consumes it in excess, then one should drink clarified butter mixed with *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (Rmañj 4.33)
Poison should never be given nor consumed during a debate;
however, it may be consumed by the teacher for the sake of inspiring confidence in the disciple.

Now, I shall explain the purification, killing, and qualities of the metals beginning with gold and ending with iron dross— along with the practical application accompanied by its proof— just as it was spoken from the mouth of my guru. (Rmañj 5.1)
One should repeatedly heat the metal and pour it seven times into each of these liquids: oil, buttermilk, cow’s urine, decoction, horse-gram water, and sour gruel. Rmañj 5.2.
The purification of substances from gold down to iron is certain;
now I shall describe both their refinement and their incineration.
Gold, having been infused for five days with clay and the acid of *mātuluṅga*,
should be purified by means of *puṭapāka* together with ashes and salt.
One should place gold equal in weight to purified mercury in a mortar and form it into a ball;
having added an equal amount of sulfur both above and below, one should then seal the whole together.
One should apply thirty vanopalas for each [application]; in this manner, fourteen puṭas are to be given.
Thus, ash that leaves no residue (niruttha) is produced; the fragrance should be applied again and again.
Having prepared gold ash, one should smear gold leaves that are thin enough to be pierced by a thorn; with mercury processed in lemon juice, the gold is killed in ten *puṭa* cycles.
One should smear the petal with either the ash of mercury or with mercury itself;
one should also smear it with asafoetida, vermilion, and red lead, equal in measure to realgar.
Having ground it with liquid gold for a day and then formed it into a ball,
one should place it at the bottom of a vessel and fill it firmly with ashes.
One should kindle the fire intensely for two nights until it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body;
then, having removed the remaining residue, three more *puṭas* should be administered.
By this method, gold becomes immeasurable and free of dross.
This elixir is strengthening, aphrodisiac, cooling, and removes consumption and other ailments. (Ramañjari 5.11)
Having added lead equal to one-sixteenth part of melted gold, one should extract it and grind it with lime juice. (Gold ash) Rmañj 5.12.
One should place an equal amount of powdered fragrance above and below that globule;
having enclosed it within a pair of earthen saucers, one should roast it with twenty pieces of vanopalā brick.

In this way, gold placed within the hollow of a sage does not attain rise again; likewise, honey and lead powder, once ground together with the juice of the *arka* plant, do not rise again. (This refers to gold ash.)
Even gold leaf is killed [as a medicinal substance] in a mere instant by that very [process].
Gold is astringent, bitter, and sweet; it is heavy and scraping.
It is aphrodisiac, a rejuvenator, strengthening, beneficial for the eyes, bestowing beauty, and pure; it grants longevity, fatness, stability of youth, clarity of speech, and memory. (Rm 5.16)
It is said to be the supreme pacifier for those afflicted by consumption and insanity;
[this is] the purification of silver, which one desiring purity should melt with a portion of the king of alkalis. (Rmañj 5.17)
Take one part of pure talaka and four parts of silver leaf;
having ground them with the juices of jambīra fruits, one should smear the silver leaves [with this paste].

Having sealed it with three layers, it should be cooked with twenty-five vanopalas; it dies [i.e., is processed], of this there is no doubt, and fragrance should be added again and again. (Rmañj 5.19)
One should take equal parts of silver ash and sulphur;
having ground them together with the milk of the *arka* plant, one should smear this onto a leaf of silver.
One should cause the silver to be digested by means of a *puṭa* [furnace]; it will certainly become dead [metal].
Having prepared a paste with mercury, one should then mix it with the silver. (Silver:: Māraṇa 3) Rmañj_5.21 //
Afterwards, one should grind the equal parts of *tāla* and *gandha* with the juice of *nimbuka*;
after two or three roastings (*puṭa*), it becomes ash, which should indeed be employed in mercurial preparations and the like.
Silver is cold, astringent, sweet, and sour; it conquers the provocation of *vāta*,
stimulates digestion, bestows strength, is unctuous, and destroys chronic indigestion.
Silver promotes longevity, destroys chronic diseases, and is an excellent agent for scraping.
(Tāmra) They say that poison is not truly poison; it is copper that is called poison.
(Copper: eight defects)
There is one defect in poison, but eight defects are proclaimed in copper.
Delusion, fainting, burning heat, perspiration, moisture, vomiting, loss of appetite, and mental anguish—these defects are like poison. (Rmañj 5.25)
Therefore, pure copper should be taken for the pacification of disease.
One should smear a copper leaf with salts and *vajradugdha*. (Copper purification)
Having heated it in fire and sprinkled it seven times with the juices of *nirguṇḍī*,
and likewise with the milky sap of *snuhī* and the juice of *arka*, the purification of copper will be accomplished.
One should boil a copper leaf with cow’s urine over a strong fire for one yāma;
it is purified, of this there is no doubt. Now, its killing is also described.
One part of mercury and two parts of sulphur should be ground with maiden’s wine for one watch; then,
placing a copper leaf equal in weight to these two inside a crucible, one should seal it shut.
Having placed it on its side together with fine clay and salt, and having deposited ashes upon the back of the vessel along with cow dung, one should cook it on the hearth for four watches.
Water should be applied again and again until it becomes cool upon one's own body; then one should crush [the substance].
There is no doubt that death occurs; this should be employed in all yogas.
One should smear copper leaves with copper ash mixed with one-fourth part of mercury;
having ground it with acid, one should apply the offering twice, both below and above.
One should heat a copper leaf strongly for one watch (yāma) inside a vessel containing a paste of *cāṅgerī*; once it has been reduced to ash, it may be employed in all medicinal formulations.

Copper leaf, ground with the juice of *jambīra* and smeared with mercury and sulfur, placed inside a shallow dish (*śarāva*) and subjected to three roastings (*tripuṭa*), undergoes dissolution. (Copper ash) Rmañj_5.34.
(The qualities of copper ash:
Copper is bitter, sour, sweet, astringent, and exceedingly cooling.
It is an elixir that destroys phlegm, bile, and wasting, as well as skin diseases and disorders of the bodily constituents;
it destroys colic and hemorrhoids, just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree. (Ramañjari 5.36)
One should likewise kill the royal alloy (rājarīti) and the metal *ghoṣa* separately, just as one does copper.
Their purification is like that of copper; like copper, it brings about excellent qualities.
(Regarding the purification of lead and tin: One should pour liquid copper over lead and tin that have been melted;
after three applications, they attain purity within a perforated crucible.
When a snake is ground with its own excrement using three "pot-caps" (*kumbhapuṭa*), that stone turns to ash; its powder removes all urinary diseases. (Māraṇa 1)
Having ground snake-ash, a cobra, and Agastya, one should smear the vessel;
that liquid [should be applied] when the snake has been liquefied, along with [the juices] derived from Vāsā and Apāmārga.
One should mix an alkaline substance there in a fourth part according to the teacher’s instruction;
one should cook it on the hearth for one *prahara*, stirring it with a ladle made of *vāsā*.
Then, having extracted that powder, one should grind it in the juice of *vāsā*;
having extracted it again, one should put it in a crucible and grind it once more with that same [juice].
In this way, after seven coatings, the nāga becomes certainly vermilion.
(The qualities of nāga ash:
Nāga situated in silver is a colorant and it removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
It removes malabsorption syndrome, skin diseases, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, consumption, and poisons.
First, one should purify the *ābhīra* [mineral] and then melt it within a crucible. (Tin:: Māraṇa 1)
Then, one should mix in a powder of apāmārga equal to a fourth part [of the total];
with a long-pointed iron ladle, one should stir that slowly.
One should continue to rub it as before until it turns to ash;
then, everything combined together shall become the color of charcoal.
The physician should place it inside a new earthen bowl and subsequently cook it over a fierce fire; thus, tin ash will certainly be produced.
Having ground tin, lead, and *arka* with *tāla* and milk, one should roast it in a *puṭa*.
By means of the bark from a dried *aśvattha* tree, it will turn to ash after being processed seven times.
(The qualities of tin: Tin is bitter and hot, dry, and slightly aggravates wind;
it destroys urinary disorders and diseases of phlegm, kills worms, and dispels delusion. (Rmañj 5.49)
Take sixteen *palas* of *triphalā* and boil it in eight times as much water until one-fourth remains;
then add five *palas* of iron to that decoction. (Ramañjuśrī-mūlakalpa 5.50)
Having heated the leaves, one should sprinkle them seven times;
in this way, the impurity arising from the mountain-born [ore] and from iron is dissolved.
Take one part of purified mercury and two parts of *bali*;
having combined these two with an equal amount of powdered essence, one should grind them with the water of *kanyākā* (datura).
Then, for two watches (yāma), one should place the globule in a copper vessel;
covering it with castor leaves, it will become warm for two watches.
Having kept it for three days within a heap of grain, one should then grind it thoroughly;
that powder, when filtered through cloth into water, floats like a swan.

Sharp, powdered, and beautiful iron, when processed until it is "dead" (calcined) so that no residue remains, should be consumed combined with the three myrobalans and honey; this is a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
One should mix cinnabar with a twelfth part of the powder of *tīkṣṇaloha*; having kneaded it with the juice of *kanyā* for two *yāmas*, one should then roast it in a *puṭa*.
Thus one should seal the iron powder; after being processed seven times, it will undergo dissolution.
One should sprinkle iron leaves with the juice of *kākodumbarikā* six times while they are being heated again and again, and then pound them in a mortar.

Having added mercury equal to one-fifth part of that [quantity], one should thoroughly rub everything together with the juice of *kumārī* (datura) and likewise place it in a "strong" (*tīkṣṇa*) or an "elephant" (*gaja*) crucible.
Diligently, one should perform this three times with decoctions of triphalā, using that same number of applications;
thus, through fourteen puṭas, the metal becomes soluble in water.

Having smeared the sword with the marrow of the *tinduka* fruit, one should place it in the hot sun using a bell-metal vessel; in a single day, it is sufficiently roasted (*puṭita*). (Iron ash). *Ramañjari* 5.60.
One should apply the ointment again and again; at the end of the day, one should grind it with a decoction of triphalā. Within a single day, death will occur.
(Iron ash:

One should repeatedly cast red-hot iron leaf into a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphala*) until it becomes powdered; then one should cook it in a decoction of the three myrobalans mixed with cow’s urine. One should roast it in a *puṭapāka* using a decoction of *matsyākṣī* and the three myrobalans until it is "non-reboundable" (*niruttha*). Afterwards, saturated with clarified butter and honey and well-roasted, it becomes iron ash.
(Regarding the examination of the *vāritara* state: All this dead iron must be smelted within the "fivefold dead" [process].
If it should thus become incapable of rising again, it truly becomes *vāritara*. (Rmañj 5.63)
(Regarding iron-based ash:
One should grind equal parts of sulfur, blue vitriol, and iron together in a mortar for one day with the juice of kanyākā; then, having sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
In this manner, the re-emergence of all metals should be performed in this way.

(The qualities of iron ash: Black iron [ash] cures colic, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, anemia, and urinary disorders; it maintains youthfulness, is heavy, beneficial for the eyes, laxative, and removes diseases of the fat tissue. Rmañj 5.65.
O living being, there is indeed nothing else equal to iron as a supreme elixir (rasāyana), for it bestows longevity, produces strength and vigor, removes disease, and brings about passion.
A practitioner of the Iron [Vow] should renounce the kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, sesame oil, black gram, and kingfisher meat,
as well as liquor and sour juices.
Whatever qualities are found in the killed *muṇḍa* are also present in the dross (*kiṭṭaka*) of *muṇḍa*.
Therefore, one should employ *maṇḍūra* everywhere for the pacification of diseases.
The best iron is that which is one hundred years old; the middling is eighty years old;
the inferior is sixty years old; anything younger than that is like poison.
Iron dross, burnt with wood from the *akṣa* tree and quenched eight times in cow’s urine, should be powdered and licked with honey; this quickly destroys consumption and jaundice in men.
O Shaven-headed One, from *kiṭṭa* [iron dross] tenfold is *muṇḍa* [mild iron]; from *muṇḍa*, *tīkṣṇa* [sharp iron] is more than a hundredfold;
and from *tīkṣṇa*, *kānta* [magnetite] is a hundred-thousandfold. Through its consumption, it produces great merit.
I perpetually pay homage to Dhanvantari, the god arisen from the ocean of milk, clad in yellow garments, four-armed, and the constant destroyer of various serpents. (Rmañj 6.1)
Just as one who has heard it from the mouth of the Guru and experienced its flavor, that very flavor is proclaimed here for the purpose of destroying disease. (Rmañj 6.2)
Except for a single physician of elixirs who possesses gain, honor, and fame,
what physician could obtain even a single cowrie shell by means of grass, wood, and medicinal herbs?
Whatever medicinal formulation for a particular disease has been proclaimed by the sages,
the physician should administer that specific formulation along with mercury (sūta).
One should not consume an excessive amount of a taste, a poison, or a medicine;
rather, one should administer the proper dose after considering the three types of humors and the state of the digestive tract.
One should add equal parts of mercury, diamond, gold, silver, lead, iron, and copper that have been killed [by processing], along with pearl, pyrites, and coral. (Ratnagarbhapaṭolī, 6.6)
Having ground conch shell in equal parts with the juice of *citraka* for seven days,
and then having powdered it, one should fill the *varāṭikā* (cowrie shells) with that.
Having ground borax with the milk of the sun-plant (Calotropis gigantea), one should seal the crucible;
then, having enclosed it within an earthen vessel, one should cook it properly in a gajapuṭa fire.
Having removed it while still warm from one's own body, one should have it made into fine powders;
then, taking all of that powder, one should perform seven saturations with *nirguṇḍī*.

It should be saturated twenty-one times with the juices of fresh ginger and twenty-one times with the decoctions of *citraka*, then dried; one should administer four *guñjā* seeds of this preparation.
It quickly destroys consumption, whether curable or incurable, without a doubt;
one should administer it with long pepper, honey, ghee, and black pepper. (Rmañj 6.11)
In cases of the eight great diseases— cough, fever, asthma, and diarrhea—
one should employ this "Jewel-Womb" poultice among those who can assimilate medicinal formulations.
(Mṛgāṅkarasa):
Gold should be equal to mercury; pearls should be double that amount;
sulphur should be equal to that [mercury]; and borax should be one-fourth the amount of mercury.
Having formed that entire mass into a ball, one should dry it with *kāñjika* (sour gruel);
then, one should cook it for four watches (*yāma*) in a vessel filled with salt.
That which is known as Mṛgāṅka should be understood as the destroyer of the king's yoga;
the physician should administer four guñjās of this along with black pepper.
Or the wise man should lick ten *pippalī* fruits with honey;
he should generally employ wholesome and very light meat as his diet. (Rmañj 6.16)
One should employ curd, ghee, products of the cow, buttermilk, or milk as food,
along with side dishes that are cooked until soft, not excessively salty, and without asafoetida.
One should avoid eggplant, oil, and bilva fruits, as well as *kāravella*, even when prepared with garlic, citron, and black pepper in a manner that does not cause acidity.
One should avoid women from afar and should also completely abandon anger;
one should boil a pala of the root of the creeper named *tumbarikā*. (Rm 6.19)
One should cause [the patient] to drink [this] combined with the three pungents for the pacification of cough;
one should boil the root of that which is known as *triśūlī* according to its strength.
One should consume a *kākiṇī* measure each of *citraka* and *vacā*, combined with a little asafoetida,
along with wholesome food, for the pacification of all diseases.
One should constantly hold in the mouth a pill made from the powder of *markaṭī* leaves mixed with honey; it destroys cough and constipation. (Rmañj 6.22)
Goat meat, goat milk, goat ghee with ginger, and the consumption of goat products—these, when taken together, destroy consumption (yakṣman) when used in the midst of goat preparations. (Rmañj 6.23)
The strength of men depends on the waste products, and their life depends on the semen;
therefore, one should especially protect the waste and the semen of a person afflicted by consumption.

One *pala* of powdered conch shell, one *pala* each of mercury and sulfur, and even a single *māṣa* of borax— one should grind these together with a *jambīra* fruit. (The Essence of the Lord of the World) Rmañj 6.25.
This supreme Lord of the World, named Puṭelo Lokeśvara,
shall conquer leprosy, blood-bile, and other diseases, and bring about the destruction of consumption.
Who else in the world besides the Lord of the World can bestow nourishing vigor and grant supreme beauty and charm, [having received them] from the mouth of Śambhu?
(Lokeśvarapaṭolī-rasa):
One should prepare gold with one-quarter part of mercury-ash;
having added double the amount of sulfur, one should grind it with the juice of *citraka*. Rmañj 6.28.
Having filled cowrie shells with borax and sealed them,
one should place the powder inside a clay vessel, draw a line around it, and close the opening.
Having dried it, one should place it in a crucible and apply fire during the afternoon;
once it has cooled to the touch of one's own body, one should extract it, powder it, and then store it away.
This is the one named Lokeśvara, who increases the nourishment of vigor; four *guñjā* seeds of this, combined with *pippalī* and honey— *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* 6.31.
One should consume this with supreme devotion; it is the Lord of the World, the bestower of all accomplishments.
This medicinal juice is effective in cases of emaciation of the limbs, sluggish digestion, cough, and bilious fever.
One should administer it for three days with saffron mixed with ghee;
during that time, one should avoid salt and sleep with the feet pointing upward.
For twenty-one days, one should drink black pepper with ghee;
wholesome food should be given like that of the moon, and one should sleep with the feet pointing upward.
Those who are withered by uneven winds, those pervaded by the disease of consumption, those afflicted with leprosy, those struck by jaundice through the methods of quack physicians,

those emaciated and ill-fated, those tormented by various fevers, and those fallen into delusion, intoxication, and madness— all these shall become free from ailment and their pains destroyed through the service of this *poṭalī*.
(Rājamṛgāṅkarasa): Three parts of the ash of mercury, one part of the ash of gold,
one part of the ash of dead copper, along with realgar, sulphur, and orpiment.
Having combined the two purified portions and ground them together,
one should fill cowrie shells with that mixture, as well as with borax dissolved in goat’s milk.
Having ground [the ingredients] with that [liquid], one should block the mouth [of the vessel] and seal it within an earthen pot.
Once dried, it should be cooked in a *gajapuṭa* fire and powdered when cooled to the touch of one's own body.
This mercury, known as *rājamṛgāṅka*, consisting of four *guñjās*, removes phlegm.
One should administer a decoction together with ten *pippalīs*, honey, nineteen black peppers, and ghee, in cases of wasting (*kṣaya*) arising from wind and phlegm. (Rmañj 6.39)
(Ratnagirirasa): Pure mercury, an equal amount of sulfur, and dead gold, mica, and copper—
each should be equal to the mercury— and dead iron should be half the amount of the mercury.
One should grind half a part of iron and dead vaikrānta with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*;
having been cooked like *parpaṭī*, it should be powdered and processed separately.
With *śigru*, *vāsaka*, *nirguṇḍī*, *vacā*, *soma*, *agni*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*; with *kṣudrā*, *amṛtā*, *jayantī*, *muni*, *brāhmī*, and *sutiktaka*.
Having treated it with three sets of three fluxes (*drāva*) and counter-fluxes (*pratidrāva*),
and having enclosed it within a small crucible (*laghupuṭa*), one should cook it in a *bhūdhara* [furnace] and then extract it.
In this case of acute fever, one should administer a dose of the juice measuring one māṣa.
Mixed with black *adhānyaka*, one becomes free from fever within a moment;
this is the elixir named Ratnagiri, which carries the power of the yoga.

One should grind equal parts of long pepper (*pippalī*), vermilion (*hiṅgula*), and poison (*viṣa*) together in a mortar. A dose of two *guñjā*s should be administered with honey for the alleviation of wind-fever (*vātajvara*). (Hiṅguleśvararasa? Rmañj 6.46.
(Śītabhañjī-rasa):
Mercury, Rasaka, Tāla, Tuttha, Ṭaṅkaṇa, and Gandhaka— all these,
purified and in equal parts, [should be macerated] for one day with the juices of Kāravelī.
One should rub that paste and smear it on the inner surface of a copper vessel to the thickness of half a finger; then one should cook it in what is called "sandy" fire.
While the grains on his back continue to burst open in the machine,
the physician should then extract the well-cooled [substance] from the interior of a copper vessel.
The juice called Śītabhañjī-rasa should be powdered with an equal amount of black pepper;
one should consume one *māṣa* of it with a leaf-fragment, and it will destroy fever—
whether irregular, acute, or occurring on the first, second, third, or fourth day— within three days.
(Śītabhañjī-rasa):
Equal parts of mercury, cinnabar, sulphur, and *jaipāla* seeds should be ground together with a decoction of *dantī*;
this elixir is known as a destroyer of fever.
Then, one should administer two *raktikās* with the juice of fresh ginger;
it destroys even most terrible acute fever within the span of a single watch (*yāma*).
Sugar, curd, and boiled rice should be diligently administered as wholesome diet;
one should drink cold water afterwards, and the juice of sugarcane and mung beans is beneficial.
This is known as *Śītabhañjīrasa*, the destroyer of all fevers.
(Śītārirasa):
Equal parts of mercury, borax, sulphur, and copper powder should be taken;
twice the amount of mercury, namely *jaipāla* seeds, should be added, ensuring they are free from husks.
Saindhava salt, black pepper, the ash of tamarind bark, and sugar—each of these should be equal in measure to mercury; one should grind them together with jambīra fruits for one day.
Two guñjas [of this] with warm water remove fever caused by wind and phlegm;
this elixir named Śītāri is supreme for curing cold-fever.
(Jvararājarasa):
One part of the king of mercury (rasarāja), and half a part of honey (mākṣika).
Two parts of stone and three parts of sulfur are prescribed;
eighteen parts of orpiment and five parts of copper.
Three parts of *bhallātaka* should all be ground together into a powder;
having soaked it in the milk of a *vajrī* plant, one should place it in a sturdy earthen vessel.
Having firmly applied the seal, one should cook it for four watches;
once it has cooled naturally, one should extract it and grind it thoroughly once again. (Rmañj 6.60)
One should administer four *guñjā* seeds of this [drug] along with a piece of its leaf;
this is the renowned "King of Fevers," the destroyer of the eight types of fever.
Having consumed this wholesome and beneficial rice with buttermilk in the morning,
combined with a portion of *tuttha*, it wards off quartan fever.
(Mahājvarāṅkuśarasa):
Equal parts of mercury, sulfur, and poison, along with an amount of dhattūra seeds equal to the sum of those three;
twice that quantity of the powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa)—two guñjās of this is beneficial.
Combined with the marrow of the jambīraka fruit and the juices of ginger,
this is called Mahājvarāṅkuśa, the destroyer of the eight types of fever.
It destroys, without a doubt, all fevers arising from the three humors— those occurring every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, and those with irregular intervals.
One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exercise, sexual intercourse, bathing, or walking as long as they have not regained their strength. (Rmañj 6.66)
(Prāṇeśvararasa):
Pure mercury, as well as sulfur, dead mica, and combined with poison.
The wise one should grind that [substance] evenly with the juice of *tālamūlī* for three days;
having filled a small jar (*kūpikā*) with it and sealed it, he should dry it thoroughly.
Then, having wrapped it with seven layers of clay and cloth, one should let it dry;
one should then fire it in a crucible the size of a jar and, once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, remove it.
Then, having taken [the ingredients] from the middle of the jar, one should grind them for a day,
including cumin, *citraka*, asafoetida, *svarjikā*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Guggulu, the five salts, yavakṣāra, yavānikā, marica, and pippalī— each of these in equal measure.
One should then saturate these seven times with their decoction in the sun;
combined with betel leaf, this Lord of Tastes (Raseśvara) consists of five guñjas.
In the case of severe acute fever, one should give [the medicine] and drink warm water afterwards;
this is the essence known as Prāṇeśvara, which subdues the provocation of *sannipāta*.
In cases of cold-fever preceded by a burning sensation, in abdominal tumors, and in colic caused by the three humors,
one should provide the desired food and apply sandalwood ointment.
The alleviation of the intensity of suffering may arise through the conversation and singing of children;
of this there is no doubt, and the man attains well-being.
(Navajvarebhasiṃharasa):
One should powder equal parts of purified mercury, sulphur, iron, copper, lead, black pepper, long pepper, and dry ginger. Rmañj 6.76.
Having added half a portion of poison, one should grind it for two days;
the physician should then administer two *guñjā* seeds with a decoction of ginger as an after-drink.
In acute fever, in most terrible [conditions], in wind disorders,
and in diseases of the digestive tract, one should employ this "Lion among New Fevers" for all diseases.
(The Pañcānanajvarāṅkuśa Rasa):

One part of the ornament from Śambhu’s throat [mercury] with black pepper, one part of the blood of Māra’s enemy [cinnabar], one part of the Sun [iron], two parts of the ocean-eyed one [sulfur], one part of the moon-joined [mica], and a portion endowed with the number of the Sun [sixteen parts of gold].

Having indeed ground these together in a mortar with the juices of the sun [juice of *arka* flowers], this perfected elixir, known as Pañcānana, which crushes the pride of the teeth of fever, is ready for use in a dose of one *guñjā*.
Wholesome food should be given—curds, buttermilk, and rice, combined with rock salt and sugar;
likewise, fragrant unguents, the drinking of cold water, milk, and auspicious pomegranate should be provided.
(Pañcānanarasa):

One should prepare pills the size of a *guñjā* seed from these ingredients—mercury, sulfur, *citraka*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *mustā*, poison, and the three myrobalans (*traiphala*)—using twice as much jaggery.

This is indeed renowned as Pañcānana, which crushes the pride of the elephant-like hosts of diseases, such as the eighteen types of leprosy, wind-pain, abdominal disorders, consumption, urinary disorders, and so forth.
(The Elixir of the Revival of the Dead):
Four parts of *mleccha*, three parts of *jaipāla* are prescribed, two parts of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and one part of *amṛta*. (Ramañjari 6.82)
The best of physicians should grind all that together finely while dry for one *yāma*;
it should be administered with ginger water along with *vyoṣa*, *citraka*, and rock salt.
A dose of two *guñjās* will certainly remove the fever; this is certain.
One should anoint [the image] with sandalwood mixed with camphor.
The physician should administer it with a bronze vessel and thus sustain the patient;
he should have him eat śāli rice together with buttermilk and combined with bilva fruit.
In cases of a most terrible combination of humors, in the threefold disorder of irregular fever, in āmavāta, in wind-pain, in abdominal tumors, in splenic disorders, and in dropsy; Rmañj 6.86.
This sovereign of elixirs (Raseśvara) should be employed in cases of fever preceded by cold or preceded by burning, in irregular or continuous fevers, in impaired digestion, and in disorders of Vāta.
This is renowned in the Ocean of Alchemy as "The Reviver of the Dead."
(Ravisundararasa):
Copper struck with a two-part rhythm (*dvibhāgatāla*), mercury, sulfur, and poison should be equal in measure.
One should add double the amount of *jayapāla* seeds; this should be done twenty-one times under the rays of the sun.
Having ground this powder with the fresh juice of *nimba*, one should take a dose of one *guñjā* combined with sugar;
this "Fever-Goad" known as *Ravisundara* destroys all eight types of fever without exception.
(The Sannipātabhairava compound:
Copper, Gandharasa, white Spanda, black pepper, Pūtana, Samīna,
Pittaja, and Jaipāla— these should be taken in equal parts and ground together.
Four *guñjā* of this [medicine] is a supreme remover of acute fever;
this "Goad for Fever" (*Jvarāṅkuśa*), the "Terrifying One for *Saṃnipāta*," has thus been revealed.
(Bhasmeśvararasa): One should take sixteen *niṣkas* of forest-stone ash (*āraṇyopalaka*), three *niṣkas* of black pepper, and one *niṣka* of poison, and grind them into a powder. (Rmañj 6.93)
This [medicine] named Bhasmeśvara destroys the *sannipāta* disorders;
one should consume it in a dose of five *guñjās* with the juice of fresh ginger.
(Pratāpalaṅkeśvara-rasa):
Having ground the powder of the root of Apāmārga with the bark of Citraka roots,
one should strain the resulting juice through a cloth.
One should grind together equal parts of sulphur,
mica, cinnabar, poison, borax, and orpiment for seven days.
One should saturate [the substance] with the tubers of *muśalī* for three days while protected from the heat;
then, having filled a crucible shaped like a cow's udder, one should seal it shut.
Having wrapped it in seven layers of clay and cloth, one should seal it lightly;
[this applies to] mercury, as well as iron, tin, silver, and copper.
Madhūkasāra, jalada, reṇukā, guggulu, śilā,
and cavyaka should each be taken in equal parts, with purified viṣa added as half a portion.
One should grind all of that in a mortar and saturate it with anti-venomous water;
one should then grind it for two *ghaṭikās* in the intense heat of the sun seven times.
With a decoction of the three pungents and the juice of *kanaka*,
with a decoction of the three fruits and the juice of *munipuṣpa*.
With the water from the fruit of the ocean, likewise with the water of victory,
with the decoction of *citraka*, and with the juice of *jvālāmukhī*.
Each [ingredient] should be processed seven times, and likewise one should process the flour;
one should fumigate the whole with poison in equal proportions.
Having then ground it for a day, one should preserve it within a small jar;
[one should take] a single *guñjā* with water from a fire-pit or with the juice of fresh ginger.
One should give it to the sick person for the sake of pacifying intense delusion and forgetfulness;
having struck the palate with a blade, one should crush [the plant] in fresh water.
When the teeth do not erupt, one should perform this rite:
having consecrated them with mantras, one should repeatedly sprinkle [the child] with water from hundreds of jars.
When that patient develops a desire for food,
one should give him rice with curd mixed with sugar, along with buttermilk and cumin.
If one desires, one may give a drink mixed with sugar;
yet even when this is done, there will be no pacification of the fever born of the [vitiated] rasa.
Make it cool with an anointing of sandalwood juice mixed with moonbeams,
and cover it with tūlikā, mallikā, jātī, punnāga, and bakula flowers.
Having prepared a bed, he should repeatedly anoint the one situated there with sandalwood pastes,
while employing amorous gestures, expressions, playful charms, speech, and glances made tremulous by side-long looks.
Through the embraces of amorous women, which press against her full and lofty breasts;
through the delightful sounds of the lute and other instruments; and through songs that are nectar to the ears.
Through auspicious conversations concerning the stories of the Purāṇas of meritorious renown,
and by these means, the supreme alleviation of suffering arises.
