One should avoid sexual intercourse as long as one has not become strong;
in cases of diseases such as wind (vāta), one should administer [medicines] with rock salt, guggulu, and fire.
One should administer it with honey and long pepper for jaundice, eye diseases, and anemia;
it should be employed in all diseases along with appropriate vehicles (anupāna) suited to each specific ailment. (Rmañj 6.114)
This Lord of Laṅkā, full of majesty, is the destroyer of the derangement of the humors.
(Mahodadhirasa:
Equal parts of mercury, sulfur, iron, poison, cowrie shells, copper, the ash of tin, and mica; Rmañj_6.116.
The three pungents, cinnamon leaf, musta, viḍaṅga, nāgakeśara,
reṇukā, āmalaka, and pippalī root.
Having diligently ground twice the amount of these [ingredients],
one should apply the medicinal saturation (*bhāvanā*) there with water infused with *gajapippalī*.
This pill is proclaimed to be the size of a chickpea;
it destroys asthma, as well as cough, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.
It removes heartache, pain in the flanks, ear diseases, and kapālika; it cures saṃgrahaṇī disease and the eight abdominal ailments,
as well as the twenty types of urinary disorders and the four kinds of urinary stones.
There is no restriction regarding food and drink, nor concerning cold, wind, travel, or sexual intercourse;
a person who delights in such activities as they please during the practice will become as fair as a heap of gold.
One part each of madodadhivaṭī and viṣasūta, two ṭaṅkas each of jātī, three of kṛṣṇā, six of viśva, and two burnt kapardikās; Rmañj_6.122.
Having diligently crushed all the *devapuṣpa* flowers measured by a *bāṇa*, the pill named Mahodadhi kindles even an extinguished fire. (Rmañj 6.123)
One should grind mercury and sulfur with the juices extracted from dhattūra fruits for one day, and then add an equal amount of the three pungent spices (trikaṭu). Rmañj 6.124.

The elixir known as "the Madman" is the destroyer of the derangement of the humors (sannipāta). What dharma has he not accomplished, and what worship does he not deserve—he who rescues the embodied being submerged in the ocean of the humors' imbalance? (Rm 6.125)
(The essence of designating names: Vacā, garlic, kaṭuka, rock salt, the fruit of bṛhatī, rudrākṣa, the heartwood of madhu, and the fruit of sāmudrakāmṛta.
One should saturate these equal parts with the milk of the *arka* plant,
then saturate them with the bile of a fish three times, and thereafter reduce them to powder.
This excellent *dhamana* (fumigation) is prescribed for extremely severe *sannipāta*,
as well as for conditions of excessive *kapha*, excessive *vāta*, epilepsy, and *halīmaka*.

In cases of diseases of the head, the ears, or the eyes, one should, according to the prescribed rite, cause [the medicine] to be administered through both nostrils; this is the supreme method for restoring consciousness.
(Candraśekhararasa):
Pure mercury, an equal amount of sulphur, black pepper, and borax; Rmañj 6.130.
Four equal parts of white [mercury] should be combined and processed with fish gall;
one should grind it for three days with that—this is the *Candraśekhara* elixir.
Two guñjas of fresh ginger juice should be administered, followed by cold water;
curd-rice and eggplant should be prescribed as wholesome diet therein.
(Kanakasundararasa):
Cinnabar, black pepper, sulfur, long pepper, borax, and poison.
One should grind seeds of gold with an equal portion of *vijayā* juices for just one watch (yāma); a pill the size of a chickpea (*caṇa*) is then prepared.
When consumed, the essence *kanakasundara* destroys the *grahaṇī* disorder;
it eliminates weak digestion, acute fever, and dysentery. (Rmañj 6.135)
For those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, buttermilk is digestive, constipating, and light;
it is wholesome because it has a sweet post-digestive effect (*pāka*) and does not provoke *pitta*.
(Rāvavāṇarasa):
One *śāṇa* each of mercury and sulfur is taken.
Cinnabar, borax, black pepper, and likewise poison—
these four medicinal substances are each said to be two ṭaṅkas.

Having combined the seed of the *jaipāla* with one *ṭaṅka* [of mercury] according to the measure of the directions, it should be rubbed with the juice of *tintiḍī*; thus a pill the size of a *guñjā* is prepared.
All types of irregular fevers, including those that recur every day, every two days, every three days, and every four days, are [subdued] when combined with *tulasī* leaves.
It swiftly destroys all [ailments] such as cold and burning;
for food, one should be given wholesome milk-rice or curd-rice.
The elixir named Rāmabāṇarasa is the destroyer of all diseases.
One should add equal parts of dead mercury, dead copper, and dead gold, along with an equal amount of the heartwood of *khadira* and likewise *mocarasa*. (Candraprabhāvaṭī) Rmañj 6.143.
One should grind the juices extracted from the roots of the *śālmalī* tree for two *praharas*;
one should then consume a pill the size of a chickpea (*caṇa*) along with one *niṣka* of cumin.
This will certainly destroy diarrhea arising from the three *doṣas*, even when accompanied by fever. (Rmañj 6.144)
(Citrāmbararasa):
One should grind equal parts of purified and calcined mercury, mica, and sulfur together;
then one should cook them for one watch (yāma) over a mild fire in an iron vessel smeared with ghee.
One should stir it with an iron rod, remove it from the fire, and let it cool;
then, having processed it with decoctions of *jīraka* for three days, a person should consume it for one month.
The juice named Citrāmbara pacifies dysentery accompanied by blood, as well as colic caused by undigested matter (āma) and dysentery with straining, when used as a vehicle.
(Grahaṇīkapāṭarasa):
One part each of pearl, silver, gold, and iron, two parts of sulfur, and three parts of mercury; one should grind these together for one day.
Then one should strongly soak the deer-horn in the fresh juices of *kapittha* and roast it using the medium *puṭapāka* method;
thereafter, having extracted it, one should grind it.
In this manner, [the ointment] is prepared seven times with the juices of *balā*, three times with the juices of *apāmārga*;
[and it contains] *lodhra*, *prativiṣā*, *mustā*, *dhātakī*, *indrayava*, and *amṛtā*.
The cultivation of each of these should be performed three times over with their respective juices;
a juice the size of a masha bean should be administered together with honey and black pepper.
This elixir named Kapāṭa destroys all types of diarrhea as well as the five forms of *grahaṇī*; it is an inflamer of the digestive fire.
(Grahaṇīkapāṭarasa):
Pearl, gold, mercury, sulphur, borax, mica, and cowrie shell in portions equal to that of "immortality" (mercury);
all these, together with powdered conch-shell, should be rubbed in a mortar with the juice of *ativiṣā*.
Having formed a ball and placed it in a clay vessel, one should seal it and cook it in a pot for half a day;
once well-cooked and cooled to the touch, this mercury (rasa) should be processed with the juices of *dhattūra*, *vahni*, and *muśalī*.
Cooked in an iron vessel, this *saṃgrahaṇīkapāṭa* becomes perfected;
it should be combined with black pepper and ghee for conditions dominated by wind (*vāta*), and with honey and long pepper (*pippalī*) for those dominated by bile (*pitta*).
In cases of *grahaṇī* where phlegm (*śleṣman*) predominates, it should be combined with the juice of *vijayā* as well as the three pungent spices (*kaṭutraya*).
In cases of wasting, fever, hemorrhoids, disorders of the feces, acute dysentery, loss of appetite,
nasal catarrh, delusion, difficulty in urination, and the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus), two *guñjās* [of this medicine] destroy even great diseases.
(Vajrakapāṭarasa):
dead mercury, mica, sulphur, barley-alkali, and borax.
The wise one should prepare agnimantha and vacā in quantities equal to the mercury;
then, one should rub it with the juices of jayantī, jambīra, and bhṛṅga.
Then, having formed a ball [of the substance] and dried it for three days, one should preserve it;
and one should place salt upon an iron vessel.
One should slowly turn the fire downwards and remove it after half a watch (yāmārdha);
one should then add ativiṣā equal in measure to the mercury, as well as mocarasa.
The physician should saturate [the medicine] seven times with the juices of *kapittha*, *vijayā*, and *adrau* (mountain ebony),
along with *dhātakī*, *indrayava*, *mustā*, *lodhra*, *bilva*, and *guḍūcī*.
Having infused this with these juices for one day, one should dry it thoroughly;
then, one should lick a single *māṣa* of this "Rasavajra" known as *kapāṭa* with honey.
One should drink equal parts of ginger, *viḍaṅga*, *bilva*, and salt with warm water; this overcomes all forms of *grahaṇī*.
(Vijayabhairavarasa): Mercury,
sulfur, iron, poison, *citraka*, mica, *viḍaṅga*,
*reṇukā*, *mustā*, cardamom, saffron, and cinnamon leaves.
The three fruits, the three pungents, and likewise copper ash.
These [ingredients] are taken in equal parts, and double the amount of jaggery (guḍa) is added;
it is used for cough, asthma, consumption, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and irregular fevers.
This pill is recommended for sluggish digestion, colic, anemia, as well as for diseases of the hands, feet, and other limbs. (Rmañj 6.167)
(The Essence of Ānandabhairava:
Cinnabar, vatsanābha poison, black pepper, borax, and long pepper.
One should powder [the ingredients] in equal proportions; this is indeed the essence of Ānandabhairava.
Having ascertained the patient's strength, one should administer it in a dose of one or two *guñjās*.
One should then lick one *karṣa* of the powdered bark of *kuṭaja* fruit with honey; this conquers diarrhea caused by the three *doṣas*. (Rmañj 6.170)
One should provide wholesome curd-rice, as well as cow's and goat's buttermilk;
for thirst, cool water is beneficial, and at night, Vijayā is salutary.
(Regarding the Meghaḍambararasa:
One should grind sulphur in equal proportion to mercury with Taṇḍulīya water,
place it inside an *andhamūṣā* crucible, and having heated it in a *bhūdharayantra*, reduce it to ashes.
One should steep [the drug] for two praharas in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla).
Two guñjas of this "Meghaḍambara" rasa quickly remove hiccup, cough, and fever; this rasa should be administered with an appropriate after-drink (anupāna). Rmañj 6.173.
(Regarding the mercury known as Triguṇākhya-rasa: Take purified mercury double the amount of sulphur and [process it] for a moment over a gentle fire.
Having cooked it, removed it from the heat, and ground it into a powder, one should consume seven *guñjā*s of that mixture combined with an equal amount of *abhayā*, increasing the dose day by day.
One should gradually increase the dose by one *guñjā* at a time until it reaches twenty-one,
and should follow a wholesome diet of *śāli* rice mixed with milk, clarified butter, and sugar.
To pacify tremors caused by wind, one should always reside in a windless place;
the elixir known as Triguṇa removes tremors from wind within three fortnights.
(Vātapurīrasa):
Mercury, gold, diamond, silver, iron, pyrite, orpiment, blue vitriol, antimony, and sea-foam, taken in equal parts; Rmañj 6.178.
One should grind one part of each of the five salts with *vajrakṣīra* for one day, then seal it and fire it in a *bhūdhara* kiln.
One should have the patient lick a single *māṣa* of [the powder] with the juice of fresh ginger to destroy wind;
one should then administer a decoction of long pepper root along with black pepper as a follow-up drink.
It destroys all disorders of the wind (vāta), such as convulsions (ākṣepaka) and others;
this elixir is renowned everywhere and is known by the name Vātaripu (the Enemy of Wind).
(Vātagajāṅkuśarasa):
Dead iron, mercury, sulfur, copper,
orpiment, honey, harītakī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, poison, the three acrids (tryūṣaṇa), agnimantha, and borax.

Having indeed ground equal parts [of the ingredients] for one day with the juices of *muṇḍī* and *nirguṇḍī*, one should consume a pill of two *guñjā*s for the pacification of all wind disorders (*vāta*). This elixir, the "Goad for the Elephant of Wind," quickly destroys both curable and incurable ailments. (Rmañj 6.183)
(Amlapittāntakara-rasa):
One should powder equal parts of mercury, mica, and iron, along with *pathyā* (harītakī).
One should lick three *māṣa* measures with honey for the pacification of *amlapitta*.
(The Alchemical Elixir of the Fire-Prince):
One should grind mercury, sulfur, and the powder of lead together with *haṃsāṅghri* water for one day in the heat; then, one should form a pill from it.
Having wrapped it in a glass vessel and secured it firmly with three layers of clay,
one should seal the opening, dry it thoroughly, and place it in what is called "sandy ground."
Then, one should gradually kindle the fire beneath it for half a day;
once it has cooled to the touch of one's body, one should extract [the substance] and add nectar equal to one-sixth part.
Then one should perfume it with half a part of long pepper (marica) and grind them together;
this is the elixir known as Agnikumāra, and its dosage is one raktikā.
Combined with the juice of betel leaves, this [preparation] destroys these diseases:
wind-disorders, consumption, asthma, cough, and the aggravation of jaundice and phlegm. (Rmañj 6.189)
Light food such as *śāli* rice is wholesome for indigestion and the disorder of the three humors (*sannipāta*);
even the application of water is praised for the alleviation of fever.
(Agnikumārarasa): Equal parts of ṭaṅkaṇa, mercury, and sulphur; three parts of poison; and [one part each of] cowrie-shell, sarjikākṣāra, māgadhī, and viśvabheṣaja. Rmañj 6.191.
One *karṣa* each of [the aforementioned ingredients] and one-eighth part of black pepper,
ground for a day with the sour juice of *jambīra* fruits, becomes "Agnikumāraka" (the Fire-Child) for the pacification of cholera, colic, wind-disorders, and weak digestion.
Take mercury,
the sun (copper), space (sulphur), and excellent iron; having ground these for three days with the juice of *dhātrī* and *akṣa*,
rub them slightly with soft *mārkaava* and two stalks of its creeper.
Indeed, this king of juices (rasarāja), the playful grace of Līlā, when licked with honey, destroys *amlapitta*;
or one may gradually consume milk together with the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and *dhātrī* fruit.
(The Essence of Manthānabhairava):
One should powder together equal parts of dead mercury, dead copper, asafoetida, root of puṣkara, rock salt, sulphur, orpiment, and borax. (Ramañjari 6.195)
One should grind it firmly for one day with the juices of *punarnavā*, *devadāru*, *nirguṇḍī*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, and bitter *kośātakī*.
One should lick a dose of one māṣa of Manthānabhairavarasa with honey for the purpose of pacifying diseases of phlegm; thereafter, one should drink a decoction of nimba.
(Kravyādarasa):
Two palas of *rasa*, two palas of *bali*, and half a pala each of copper and iron;
having pulverized all these together, they should be cast into a heated [mold] by means of fire and placed upon castor leaves.
Then, having ground that *parpaṭikā*, one should place it in a vessel of iron purified by an excellent rite;
having added a hundred palas of ripe *jambīra* juice, which is merely sour, one should apply fire to it.
When the liquid has been digested, this [substance] should be infused with these [ingredients], along with abundant water derived from *pañcakola*,
and one hundred parts of well-roasted *ṭaṅkaṇa* powder, equal in measure, together with sour *vetasa*.
Equal parts of viḍa salt, dāruharidrā, and black pepper, soaked seven times in the sour water of fermented chickpeas (*caṇakāmlavāri*),

constitute the well-known *rasa* called *kravyāda*, as taught by Sumanthānaka and Bhairava. Two *māṣa* measures of this, drunk with rock salt and buttermilk at the end of a meal, is indeed most beneficial.

It is well known that heavy meats, milks, flour-based preparations, ghees, edibles, and fruits— even when consumed in quantities exceeding the proper measure— are digested within two watches (yāma) by its power.
Pure mercury, poison, sulfur, ajamodā, the three fruits,
sarjikṣāra, yavakṣāra, fire-salt (citraka), rock salt, and cumin; (Agnituṇḍīvaṭī).
One should grind together equal parts of sauvarcala salt, viḍaṅga, sea salt, and ṭaṅkaṇa,
along with an amount of viṣamuṣṭi equal to the total, using the acidic juice of jambīra fruit.
One should consume a pill with the luster of a mirage to pacify the dullness of the digestive fire.
(The Essence of the Arising of Bliss): Mercury, sulphur, iron, mica, and poison—each in equal parts—and black pepper eight times [the total], with borax four times [the total]. Rmañj 6.206.
Having undergone seven saturations with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and sour pomegranates,
two *guñjā* seeds, when consumed in the evening along with pieces of leaf, destroy [diseases].
By practicing this for even a short time, one shall conquer diseases arising from wind and phlegm, as well as weak digestion, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, fever, loss of appetite, and jaundice.
(Cintāmaṇirasa):
One should grind together mercury, sulfur, dead copper, dead mica, the three fruits,
the three pungents, seeds, and jayapāla in equal parts within a mortar.
This dried substance should be infused with the juices of *droṇapuṣpī* and strained through cloth;
this "cintāmaṇi" elixir is also praised for those suffering from indigestion.
It destroys the eight types of fever and is recommended for all kinds of pain; a single *guñjā* or two *guñjās* is a supreme remedy for diseases caused by undigested matter (*āma*).
(Rājavallabharasa):
One niṣka of mercury, one niṣka of sulphur, and one niṣka [of other ingredients] constitute the "Kindler" (pradīpana) elixir.
The physician should add one and a half palas of *cūlikālavaṇa* (sochal salt) and grind it in a mortar;
he should then strain it through a dry cloth.
A dose of one *māṣa* should be administered; it digests meat, fish, and other foods.
This "Beloved of Kings" should be given in cases of indigestion caused by the three *doṣas*.
(Trinetrākhyarasa):
Having ground together borax, deer-horn, gold, copper, and mercury killed [with mercury],
one should rub it for one day with the juice of ginger, seal it, and cook it in a *puṭa*.
One should take one *māṣa* of the elixir named *Trinetrāka* with honey and clarified butter;
thereafter, one should lick rock salt, cumin, and asafoetida with honey and ghee.
This is renowned for curing colic pain of digestion within just one *yāma*; of this there is no doubt. (Rmañj 6.216)
(Mehavajrarasa: Ashes, mercury, dead iron, copper ash, śilājatu, purified tāpya, manaḥśilā, the three pungents (vyoṣa), triphalā, and the seeds of aṅkola. Rmañj 6.217.
One should saturate the powder of *kapittha* and turmeric with *bhṛṅgarāja* twenty times, dry it thoroughly, and then always lick it mixed with honey.
A patient suffering from urinary disorders should lick one *niṣka* of this great elixir, "Mehevajra.
One should grind one *karṣa* of the seeds of *mahānimba*.
Having combined one *pala* of [the herb] with rice-water and two *niṣkas* of clarified butter, one should drink the liquid; it destroys urinary disorders that have arisen long ago. (Rmañj 6.220)
(Indravaṭī-rasa):
One should grind equal parts of dead mercury, dead tin, and the bark of the Arjuna tree together in a mortar with the juices extracted from the roots of the Śālmali tree.

At the end of the day, a pill the size of a *māṣa* bean should be prepared; this, known by the name Indravaṭī, destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*) and brings about the pacification of diabetes (*madhumeha*). Rmañj 6.222.
(Rasendramaṅgalarasa): Killed tāla-sattva, killed copper, killed iron, killed mercury,
killed mica, killed silver, sulphur, blue vitriol, and realgar.
Sauvīrāñjana, kāsīsa, nīlī, bhallātaka, śilājatu, arka root, kadalī-kanda, and citraka; Rm 6.224.
The black bark of the *aṅkola* tree, the root of the black datura (*kṛṣṇadhattūra*),
the seeds of *avalguja*, and the fruits of the white *mādhvī*.
Hemāhvā, phenajāti, phalinī, and viṣatinduka;
the oils, iron dross, and that which is ancient—this is amṛta.
The skin of the *mīnakākṣa* fish and its meat, each separately,
as well as *tailinya* and *vaṭaka*— one should grind all these together into a powder.
Having placed [the ingredients] in a mortar, this [mixture] should be administered;
furthermore, their infusion (bhāvanā) should be prepared with *brahmadaṇḍī*, *śikhāpuṅkhā*, *devadālī*, and *nīlikā*.
Vāṇa, śoṇā, nṛpataru, nimbasāra, vibhītaka, karañja, bhṛṅgarāja, gāyatrī, and the fruit of the tintiḍī.
The root of *malayū* should be given for these [medicines] in three portions each;
having made them into a powder and properly dried them in the sun.
One should place that vessel in another vessel and have it sealed;
then this mercury should be cooked for one watch (yāma) over a mild fire within a *puṭa*.
It certainly destroys the *puṇḍarīka* [disease]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Within two months, one should not feed men anything unwholesome.
All diseases and all forms of leprosy dissolve away for those who are constantly engaged in devotion to the Sun and who practice devotion to the Guru.
This elixir, named Rasendramangala, has been revealed by Śiva, whose nature is compassion, for the sake of favoring his devotees. (Rmañj 6.234)
(Sarveśvararasa):
Take one *pala* each of mercury, copper, mica, iron, and cinnabar (*hiṅgula*), along with *jambīra*, *unmatta*, *bhārgī*, *snuhī*, *arka*, and *viṣamuṣṭi*. Rmañj_6.235 //
It should be rubbed individually with the juices of the enemies of horses (honey) for one day at a time;
thus it should be rubbed for seven days, and that ball should be wrapped in cloth.
It should be sweated for three days in a sand-bath (*vālukāyantra*) over a mild fire;
then, having taken it all, one should grind it into powder and add one *pala* of poison.
One should have the patient lick two *guñjā* of this "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*) elixir mixed with two *pala* of powdered long pepper and honey; it cures the *kuṣṭha* known as *munimaṇḍala*.
One should lick one karṣa each of powdered vākucī and dāru;
taking it with castor oil as an after-drink (anupāna) brings comfort.
When there is an excess of blood, venesection should be performed on the foot, the arm, or the forehead;
this is especially necessary for those suffering from eye diseases and leprosy.
For a strong-bodied person who has many humors and is in the prime of life,
they maintain that this quantity— one *prastha*— is the proper measure for bloodletting.
One should know that the three times for using weapons are: during the rainy season when it is cloudless, during the summer when it is cold, and at midday during the winter season.
(1) Taleśvararasa:
Twelve *karṣas* of *tāla* [mineral] should be sweated in a *dolikāyantra* within a vessel filled with the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* until no water remains.
Afterwards, one should dry it in a mortar and add two karṣas of mercury;
one should rub it repeatedly until it becomes like collyrium.
Snuhī-milk, sunflower-milk, goat’s milk, gokṣura, vākucī, pātālagaruḍa, aṅkola, cakramarda, and hijjala; Rmañj_6.245.
Kumārī, unmatta, bhallātaka, triphalā, ambu, punarnavā,
and nimba bark— with these medicinal substances, one should perform three applications of *puṭapāka* for each.
One should place six karṣas of powdered *kalikā* in a cauldron;
having set a quarter part at the bottom, one should place the *tālaka* in the middle.
Afterwards, one should carefully place all the powder on top,
up to the rim of the pot, by means of the application of the juice of *kumārī*.
Then one should fill it and, with great effort, make the seal firm;
having placed a stone upon it, it should be so solid that it does not move.
Having extracted [the mercury] while it is still warm from its own body using the lamp-fire for four watches and the *haṭha*-fire for twenty watches, this is the *tāleśvara* elixir for leprosy.
This supreme remedy for the destruction of leprosy was proclaimed by the yogi Bhairavānanda;
in this case, the physician should prescribe green gram soup and śāli rice as wholesome diet.
(Tāleśvararasa [2]):
two parts of mercury, three of *valguja*, three of *kaṇā*, and three each of *viśvā* and *trika*.
One and a half parts of *brahmaputra*, four parts of *marica*, one part each of *nimba* and *dhattūra* seeds, and three parts of *gandhaka*. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 6.253)
Ten parts each of realgar, borax, and orpiment are prescribed;
having ground them all together with skillful means, they are then saturated with the fresh juice of the amṛtā plant.
Having dried it seven times, one should then apply dhattūra;
having ground it into a moist ball, one should wrap it with the leaves of the dhattūra plant.
One should wrap it in cow dung and cook it in a crucible known as *kukkuṭapuṭa*;
this mercury, which removes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), should be consumed at all times by those who delight in their food.
(Svarṇakṣīrī-rasa): Having thrown five palas of Hemāhvā into a jar of buttermilk, one should cook it;
once the buttermilk is digested [absorbed], one should extract it and cook it again in a jar of milk. (Rmañj 6.257)
When the milk has been digested, one should extract [the solid residue], wash it, and dry it thoroughly;
then, having powdered it, take five palas of that and two palas of black pepper.
Having combined one *pala* of mercury with one *niṣka* of *mūrchita* [mercury], one who suffers from *supti-kuṣṭha* should consume it; for this is the essence of *svarṇakṣīrī*.
(Śūlagajakesarī-rasa):
One should firmly grind purified mercury with twice its amount of sulfur for one prahara;
then, having added an equal amount of copper ash, one should seal it within a *sampuṭa* vessel.
Having added salt from above and below, the physician should place it in an earthen vessel;
then, having cooked it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, he should remove it once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body.
One should grind asafoetida, dry ginger, and cumin together into a fine powder; for the sake of relieving the pain of colic, one should consume two *guñjā* seeds of this mixture with a leaf-fragment.
One should drink one *karṣa* of powder made from *vacā* and black pepper with warm water;
this elixir, known as Śūlakesarī, shall cure even an incurable colic.
A person suffering from colic should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, alcohol, salt, pungent foods, the suppression of natural urges, and the retention of semen.
(Regarding *brahmarasa*): One part of mercury that has been processed (*mūrchita*), along with powdered *gandha*, *avalguja*, *citraka*,
and seeds of *brahma* in twelve parts each.
Thirty parts of jaggery and honey are made into pills;
this is known by the name Brahmarasa, which destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
By consuming two niṣkas of this, one destroys numbness and circular patches of leprosy;
one should drink it afterwards, having ground the root of pātālagaruḍī in water.
(Indudhararasa): Pure mercury, equal parts of sulfur, blue vitriol, and copper oxide,
ground with a decoction of *vākucī* for one day and formed into pills.
One should always consume one *niṣka* of this mercury which bears the white mark of the moon;
thereafter, one should administer one *karṣa* of *vākucī* oil along with honey as an after-drink.
(Paribhadrarasa):
One should take mercury in a state of fusion (*mūrchita*), along with *dhātrī* fruit and *nimba*;
having ground these in equal parts for one day with a decoction of *khadira*, one should consume it.
The juice called pāribhadra, weighing one niṣka, destroys ringworm and leprosy.
(Śvetārirasa): Pure mercury, equal parts of sulphur, triphalā, mica, vākucī,
bhallātaka, realgar, black pepper, and nimba seeds— each taken in equal measure.
One should grind [the substance] with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, pounding and drying it again and again;
by doing this for twenty-one days, the mercury becomes the "enemy of white" (*śvetāri*).
One should eat a niṣka of this with honey and clarified butter; it destroys white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha).
(The essence of Kālāgnirudra: Mercury, mica, the ashes of copper and steel, pyrite,
and sulphur should be ground with the juice of Vandhyākarkoṭakī for a period of one day.
Having placed [the substance] in the root of the *vandhyākarkoṭakī* plant and smeared the exterior with clay,
it should be cooked for one day in a crucible called *bhūdhara*, and then ground into a powder.
One should add a tenth part of poison and consume a dose of one *māṣa*;
this elixir, Kālāgnirudra, removes spreading skin diseases (*visarpa*) within ten days.
One should prescribe honey combined with long pepper as a post-medicine (*anupāna*).
[Then, for] Makaradhvajarasa:
one should grind mercury eight times the weight of gold together with two parts of sulphur. *Rasamañjarī* 6.277.
Then, for three days, one should place red cotton flowers from a virgin girl inside a glass jar,
dry them, seal them, and subject them to intense heat in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra).
One should reduce the lord of mercury (rasendra) to ashes, resembling the rays of the newly risen sun;
of this [ash] there is one part, and four very beautiful parts of camphor.
Then one should mix cloves, black pepper, nutmeg, and camphor in small quantities, along with musk weighing one gadyāṇaka.
When finely ground, this glorious essence becomes the god Makaradhvaja;
one or two *valla*s of it, combined with a betel leaf, [should be consumed].
One should eat sweet, unctuous, light meat that is not wind-increasing,
as well as boiled milk cooled and mixed with sugar, wheat, and ghee.
Māṣa beans, other types of flour,
and various kinds of intoxicants increase the digestive fire of men and destroy wrinkles and graying hair.
It generates intelligence, longevity, and beauty; it is a great stimulant for passion;
through practice, the adept constantly conquers a hundred women.
This supreme rasa should be enjoyed again either at the time of passion or at its conclusion;
it certainly brings about the loss of intoxication in women.
Artificial poisons, whether stationary (sthāvara), mobile (jaṅgama), or born from poisonous water,
do not cause any adverse effects for practitioners after one year.
Just as Mṛtyuñjaya conquers death for embodied beings through practice,
so too does this [mantra] destroy old age and death for the sovereign practitioner.
(Madanakāmadevarasa):
One should prepare these in their respective proportions: pearl, diamond, gold, copper, mercury, sulphur, and iron, each increasing in quantity in successive order. Rmañj 6.288.
Having ground it with the juices of *kanyākā*, one should place it in a glass jar;
sealed inside a cooking pot filled with rock salt, one should maintain it there.
One should properly seal the vessel and then place it upon the hearth;
one should apply the fire very gradually for one day, and thereafter remove it.
Having ground these until they are cool to the touch, one should saturate them with the milky sap of the *arka* plant;
[the ingredients are] *aśvagandhā*, *kaṅkolī*, *vānarī*, *muśalī*, and *ikṣura*.
One should saturate it three times with the juice of *śatāvarī* and then saturate it once with the juices of the lotus root (*padmakaṇḍa*) and *kaseru*.
One should mix musk, the three pungents (vyoṣa), camphor, kaṅkola, cardamom, and cloves—
each measured as one-eighth part of the previously mentioned powder— into that mixture.
Having added equal parts of all [the aforementioned ingredients] and sugar, one should give a measure of one *śāṇa* along with two *palas* of cow’s milk for those who consume a sweet diet.
Through its power, beauty, strength, and splendor increase;
many young women take delight [in him], and no loss of virility occurs.
Having ground pure mercury for one fortnight with juices extracted from *śālmali* trees,
one should cook it for two *yāmas* in clarified butter; then, having bound it in a cloth, one should grind it again.
Having ground it for one day with the juices of the *śālmalī* tree,
one should form it into pills, wrap them in *nāgavallī* leaf, and place them in a glass vessel.

One should cook a vessel filled with the juice of the *śālmalī* tree for two watches (yāmas) inside a sand-vessel apparatus (*vālukāyantra*); once the liquid has been digested [by heat], one should remove it.
One should consume two guñjas of musalī with sugar between the leaves of the betel vine (nāgavallī) in the morning,
and afterwards one should drink one pala of milk.
This elixir named Pūrṇendu will truly bestow virility;
a man shall certainly desire even a thousand women. (Rmañj 6.300)
Equal parts of pure mercury and sulfur, rubbed for three days with the juice of white water-lilies,
should be cooked in a *vālukāyantra* for four watches (*yāmas*) until it reaches the state of a *kūpī*.
One should saturate it for one day with the juices of *raktāṅga* mixed with sugar;
thereafter, one may eat as desired and desire a hundred women.

One should grind pure mercury and an equal amount of sulfur with the juice of red lotus petals for one watch (yāma); then, one should add half as much sulfur again as was previously used. (Madanodayarasa) Rmañj 6.303.
One should grind that for one day, and then grind it with the fragrant substance (gandha) again;
having sealed it in a glass flask for one day with the previous liquids.
Having cooked it for one day in a sand-bath (vālukāyantra) and then extracted it, one should consume this elixir called Madanodaya along with five guñjās of white sugar. Rmañj 6.305.

The seeds of the vānarī plant with their roots, along with *muśalī* and sugar in equal parts, should be drunk with cow’s milk; half a *pala* of this should be taken as a post-medicinal draught (*anupāna*).
(Anaṅgasundararasa):
Two palas each of pure mercury and likewise sulphur,
one karṣa of dead gold, and one pala of dead copper.
One should grind four *niṣkas* of dead silver with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for one day;
having then sealed it in a crucible, one should subsequently extract it after one day.
Having ground these with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should fashion a pill in the shape of a jujube fruit;
it is named Anaṅgasundara and is the supreme bestower of nourishment. (Rmañj 6.309)
(Kāmeśvararasa:

Well-reduced mica, *kaṭphala*, *kuṣṭha*, *aśvagandhā*, *amṛtā*, *methī*, *mocarasa*, *vidārī*, *muśalī*, *gokṣūraka*, *kṣūraka*, the bulb of *rambhā*, *śatāvarī*, *ajamodā*, *māṣa*, sesame, *dhānyaka*, *yaṣṭī*, *nāgabalā*, *kacūra*, *madana*, *jātīphala*, and rock salt. Rmañj_6.310 //

One should powder equal parts of bhārṅgī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the two types of cumin (jīra), citraka, the four aromatics (cāturjāta), punarnavā, gajakaṇā, grapes (drākṣā), śaṭī, vāsaka, śālmalī, andrī, the three myrobalans (phalatrika), and the seeds of the monkey-pomegranate (kapibhava). To this powder, one should add twice its weight of vijayā and sugar; then, having formed it into a bolus with honey and clarified butter— Rmañj 6.311.

A pill or electuary weighing half a *karṣa* should be consumed at all times in every way; or rather, milk with sugar should be drunk, for it is an aphrodisiac, an arrestant of emission, and a subduer of women.
It brings women under one's control, bestows supreme pleasure, and induces arousal in mature women. It provides nourishment when one is emaciated, cures consumption, and destroys all diseases.

It pacifies cough, asthma, and severe diarrhea; it kindles the weak digestive fire and increases the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). There is nothing superior to this excellent elixir (*rasāyana*). It dispels hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), urinary disorders (*prameha*), accumulations, phlegm, and excessive blood. It bestows eternal bliss upon those who possess specialized knowledge, arising from the playful eloquence of their speech. (Rmañj 6.313)

Through practice, Kāmeśvara destroys the decay of old age within a year; he who was proclaimed by the illustrious Vaidyanātha as the benefactor of all, who restores the rising passion of the elderly during union with mature women, and who is like a lion—this one of even vision and proven efficacy should always be served by kings. (Ramañjunāthīya 6.314)
(Ajīrṇakaṇṭakarasa):
One should powder pure mercury, poison,
and sulphur in equal parts, along with black pepper in an amount equal to the total, using the juice of the fruits of *kaṇṭakārī*.
One should grind and saturate all [the ingredients] twenty-one times;
one should eat a pill the size of three *guñjā* seeds for the pacification of all indigestion.
(Regarding Udayabhāskara-rasa:
One should take ten parts of copper killed with sulphur;
there should be five parts of ūṣaṇa and two parts of amṛta. Rmañj 6.317.
All of this, finely ground into powder, should be administered in the measure of one *raktikā* to a person suffering from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), properly combined with suitable adjuncts.
It is effective for boils, as well as for cholera and mandalaka,
and for the pacification of scabies, ringworm, smallpox, and the eight types of leprosy.
(The Furious Sentiment: Pure mercury and an equal amount of sulfur should be ground for four watches (yāmas),
combined with the juices of betel leaf, meghanāda, and punarnavā.
Having ground [the ingredients] in cow’s urine mixed with long pepper and sealed [the vessel], one should roast it in a mild fire;
this fierce elixir, taken in a dose of one *guñjā* with honey, conquers tumors.

(With eternally arisen rasa: Take equal parts each of dead mercury, copper, iron, mica, poison, and sulfur; and an amount of bhallātaka fruit equal to the sum of all these—grind them together into a powder.
One should grind the juices extracted from the suraṇa tuber in a mortar for three days;
by licking a dose of one māṣa with clarified butter, this elixir will destroy hemorrhoids.
The rasa, eternally arisen, is named Gudodbhavakulāntaka;
it is present in the hands, the feet, the mouth, the navel, as well as in the anus and the testicles.

For one who suffers from swelling, pain in the heart, and pain in the flanks, the treatment prescribed by Śaṅkara for incurable hemorrhoids is beneficial; indeed, even for an incurable case, this therapy should be performed.
(Arśakuṭhārarasa):
One *pala* of purified mercury, two *palas* of purified sulfur, three *palas* each of killed copper and killed iron. Rmañj 6.326.
One should add two palas each of trikaṭu, lāṅgalī, dantī, pīluka, and likewise citraka, as well as yavakṣāra and ṭaṅkaṇa.
Both [the two substances] should be combined in five-pala portions, along with five palas of rock salt (saindhava),
twenty-two palas of cow’s urine, and an equal amount of snuhī milk.
One should cook everything in a pot over a mild fire until it forms a well-kneaded mass;
one should always eat two *māṣa* measures of this, for even its juice is an axe to the hemorrhoids.
(Vidyādhararasa):
One should grind together equal parts of sulfur, realgar, pyrite, dead copper, and realgar, along with purified mercury, and then macerate them for one day.
One should saturate [the medicine] with a decoction of *pippalī* and the milk of *vajrī*;
one should then consume a *valla* with honey to conquer spleen disorders, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and other ailments. (Rmañj 6.331)
The elixir named Vidyādhara should be followed by drinking cow’s milk;
[this is] Vaṅgeśvara-rasa.
One should prepare one part each of mercury ash and tin ash. (Rmañj 6.332)
Take sulphur and dead copper, each four times [the quantity of the base metal];
grind them all together with the milk of *arka* for one day, and then form it into a ball.
Having sealed it within that earthen vessel, one should cook it and extract it with a single *puṭa* (herb-pouch) application;
thus, the substance known as Vaṅgeśvara conquers splenomegaly, abdominal tumors, and dropsy.
One should lick two *guñjā* seeds with clarified butter, or one *niṣka* of white *punarnavā*;
thereafter, one should drink *rajanī* with cow’s urine, or [the aforementioned substance] with cow’s water.

(Regarding the *udarārirasa*): One should grind mercury, green vitriol (*śikhituttha*), *jaipāla*, and long pepper in equal parts, along with the marrow of the fruits of *āragvadha*, using the milk of *vajrī*. Rmañj 6.336.
One should eat a pill the size of a black gram (*māṣa*); it removes ascites in women.
Afterward, the juice of *ciñcā* fruit is beneficial, and curd-rice is wholesome.
Indeed, this [remedy] removes ascites through a powerful purgative.
(Jalodarārirasaḥ):
Long pepper, black pepper, copper, and combined with the powder of *kāñcanī*.
One should grind *tuttha* (copper sulfate) and *jaipāla* seeds with the milky sap of *snuhī* for one day;
by consuming one *niṣka* of this, purgation occurs, which immediately destroys dropsy (*jalodara*).
For all types of purgatives, curd-rice is beneficial as a stabilizing agent;
at the end of the day, food or mung bean soup should be administered.
Take one part of mercury, one part of iron filings, one part of borax, one part of black pepper equal to the mercury,
and two parts each of sulfur, long pepper, and ginger; these should be powdered together.
One should add an equal amount of dehusked dantī seeds;
this great elixir, known as Nārāca, is perfected for purgation at a dose of two guñjas.
It destroys abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement; one should drink it with warm water.
(Icchābhedī-rasa):

One part each of mercury, sulphur, and borax, combined with ginger and black pepper; jaipāla is said to be three times [the amount of] all these, and one should grind everything together into a powder. Rmañj 6.343.
The *icchābhedi* consists of two *guñjās*; one should administer it together with sugar.
One should drink it as long as there is heat in the stomach, and through that many repetitions, one will undergo purgation.
One should provide buttermilk-rice according to one's desire, for it breaks down cravings;
the humors, though sometimes provoked, are subdued by fasting and digestive treatments.
Having prostrated before the fearless Lord, the god of the sky, the master of the world— naked as the directions, three-eyed, and the destroyer of old age and death— Rmañj [says]: Rmañj_7.1.
Both nectar and poison have been declared by Śiva to be elixirs;
when conjoined with the proper ritual procedure it is nectar, but devoid of that procedure, it is poison.
At the conclusion of the purgation, this should be consumed to eliminate all defects;
first, the wise one should eat dead mercury for one month.
Thereafter, however, for one who desires to "cultivate the field" (kṣetrīkaraṇa) within the body, one should apply [the mercury];
for in the cultivation of the field, even the immortal elixir (sūta) becomes poison.
Whence can there be the attainment of fruit for that [person], just as for a good seed in saline soil? O Goddess, one should not perform any elixir (*rasāyana*) merely by preparing the field;
indeed, the preparation of the field must be performed in every elixir practice.
Having ground the ash-mercury and sulfur in two parts for a moment with a maiden, one should seal it in a small crucible and cook it; then, having removed it, [one should mix it] with honey and ghee.

One should eat a niṣka of this; it destroys old age and death. The elixir of the "fragrant nectar" (gandhāmṛta-rasa) [is as follows]: one should powder the *bhṛṅgarāja* plant together with its roots, having dried it in the shade. Rmañj 7.7.
Equal to that should be the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā), and sugar should be the same amount as all of them combined.
One should consume one pala of this afterwards; it removes death and disease.
(Regarding Hemasundararasa:
One should prepare gold ash in a quantity equal to one-fourth part of the dead mercury.
One should have [the practitioner] lick a single māṣa of milk, clarified butter, and honey mixed together in a bronze vessel for six months; this destroys old age and death. (Rmañj 7.10)
One should daily lick one karṣa of vākucī powder saturated with the juice of dhātrī as an after-drink; thus the mercury becomes as beautiful as gold.
(The Life-Reviving Pill):
One should firmly grind purified mercury, diamond ash, the essence of mica and orpiment, iron from magnetite, and gold, equal in measure, within a *jambīra* fruit.
Having prepared a medicinal ball (*gola*) with all ingredients in equal proportions, one should extract it after seven days;
[this is done] with *gojihvā*, *vāyasī*, *vandhyā*, *nirguṇḍī*, honey, and rock salt.
One should smear the interior of a vajra-mūṣā crucible and place the *golaka* (globule) therein;
having covered it with that paste, one should cook it for one fortnight in a *bhūdhara* (earth-pressing) furnace.
Having repeatedly extracted [the substance] for each watch of the night and smeared it onto the crucible, and having sealed it as before, one should cook it; after a fortnight, one should extract it.
One should smear the crucible with *yavaciñcā*, *palāśa*, *rājī*, cotton, and rice; one should then place the pill therein.
Having added borax and white glass, and having heated it very firmly for one watch using khadira charcoal, this mercury becomes liquefied.
One should digest gold equally with the *biḍa* preparation in a crucible;
then, it should be ground for one day with cow’s urine and *triyāmaka*.
When heated in a blind crucible, it becomes bound like a diamond;
this pill, named *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī*, resides within the mouth of the crooked tube.
A dose of one karṣa destroys old age and death; this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
It also effects the paralysis of weapons, and a person attains a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā.
(Vīryarodhinī-guṭikā):
One should grind purified mercury for seven days with the juice of betel leaves and wash it with acidic liquids; [the resulting mass] shall measure four niṣkas.
Having placed it within a bulbous root of poison, one should suppress it with poison itself;
then, having placed it inside a pig's carcass, one should sprinkle it.
Having offered the bali-oblation at twilight together with a hen and vāruṇī wine,
one should then [place it] in oil mixed with dhattūra in an iron vessel upon the hearth.
Having cast it into thirty palas [of liquid], one should cook that meat-ball in its juice over a gentle fire, beginning at twilight until sunrise. (Rmañj 7.24)
One should force oneself to stay awake; otherwise, one will not attain success.
In the morning, having extracted the pill, one should place it in a vessel of milk.
That milk dries up quickly; this is the cause of that effect.
At the time of sexual union, a pill that obstructs semen should be held in the mouth.
Having drunk milk, he should enjoy a woman who is filled with passion and belongs to a noble family;
then, holding his own semen in his hand from his mouth, he emits it.
Now, for one whose humors have fully ripened, one should apply the prescribed collyrium;
collyrium is desired at midday during both the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. (Rmañj 8.1)
It is desired [to be performed] in the forenoon and the afternoon during summer and autumn;
one should always perform it during the rainy season, or indeed during the spring when it is very hot.
Collyrium is not recommended for one who is exhausted, weeping, terrified, intoxicated by liquor, suffering from a recent fever, indigestion, or the suppression of natural urges.
The physician should prepare a wick for sharp collyrium the size of a mustard seed;
the medium measurement should be one and a half times that, and it should be double for mild collyrium.
Sūtaka, sulphur, and Peta, combined with the juice of cāṅgerī, form an ointment that grants vision to men and destroys eye diseases. (Rmañj 8.5)
Equal parts of mercury and snake-ash, with collyrium twice that amount,
and camphor equal to one-fourth of the mercury— this collyrium is an elixir for the eyes.
The fat of a black cobra, conch shell, kataka nut, kaṭphala, and collyrium— these,
along with the juice of black pepper, provide supreme vision for those who are blind.
Take four parts of conch shell, half of that amount of realgar, half of the realgar of black pepper, and half of the black pepper of long pepper. Rmañj 8.8.
It destroys *timira* with water, destroys *arbuda* with brain-matter,
destroys *cipiṭa* with honey, and [destroys] *puṣpaka* with women’s milk.
Having rubbed the tips of *apāmārga* stalks with honey and rock salt,
and applying them to the eyes in a copper vessel, it thoroughly alleviates eye pain.
One should grind together the teeth of an elephant, a boar, a camel, a cow, a horse, a goat, and a donkey, along with conch shell, pearl, and sea-foam; a suppository made from all these,
when finely ground, destroys semen and is an excellent cure for seminal disorders.
One should grind together tuttha, honey, rock salt, śivā, conch shell, realgar, the water-foam of red ochre, and black pepper. Rmañj 8.12.
Having combined these with honey, one should prepare this medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) for those with blindness;
it is supreme for removing diseases of the eyelids, cataracts (*timira*), and white opacities (*kāca-śukra*). (Rmañj 8.13)
The marrow of the Śaṅkhanābhi and Vibhītaka, Pathyā, Manaḥśilā, Pippalī, Marica, Kuṣṭha, and Vacā—these should be taken in equal parts. (Rm 8.14)
Having ground [the ingredients] with goat’s milk and formed a wick of the appropriate size,
one should rub it with water in the measure of a *hareṇu* seed and then apply it as a collyrium.
The Varticandrodayā [formula] conquers cataract, fleshy growths, ophthalmia, film, tumors, night-blindness, seasonal blindness, and pupillary opacities.
When the pure lead has been melted, one should pour in an equal amount of pure mercury;
then, adding an equal amount of black collyrium to those two, one should grind everything together into a powder.
One should add camphor in a tenth part to this powder;
this is a counter-unguent that conquers eye diseases, an ambrosia for the eyes.
If, after eating and rubbing one's palms together, [the ointment] is applied to the eyes,
any diseases that have arisen will perish and shall never recur.
By washing the eyes with a decoction of triphalā every morning,
that water will soon dispel all cataracts.
One should grind equal parts of triphalā and iron powder with water;
then one should cook them for a moment over a mild fire with an amount of oil equal to the weight of those two combined.
One should cook that oil with an equal amount of *bhṛṅga* juice;
having placed it in a greased vessel, one should leave it in the ground for a month and then extract it.
One should apply [the paste] for seven days after wrapping the head with plantain leaves;
one should eat a milk diet in a windless place and wash [the head] with water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should always perform this for seven days;
it will become a dye that lasts for as long as one lives, without a doubt, and the hair will become like a black bee.
One should take equal parts of *kākamācī*, barley, jasmine, and black sesame seeds; having extracted that oil by means of a press, it serves for the coloring of the hair.

A man who always bathes with the paste of iron-rust and *āmalaka* along with *japā* flowers will here destroy his graying hairs, just as one who bathes in the Gaṅgā destroys the flood of hellish rebirths.

Having prepared oil cooked with the root of *kāśmarya*, the flower of *sahacara*, the root of *ketakī*, iron powder, and *bhṛṅgarāja*, combined with water from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), one should place it in an iron vessel and bury it in the ground for one month. By merely applying this, hair that was once as white as *kāśa* grass becomes black, resembling a swarm of bees.
One should saturate very white sesame seeds with *vajrī* milk for seven days;
when the hair is anointed with the resulting oil, it will indeed become white—of this there is no doubt. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 8.28)
Rmañj 9:
Having ground together equal parts of camphor, borax, mercury, and the juice of *munī* with honey, one should smear it upon the *liṅga* and remain there for one watch (three hours). Rmañj_9.1.
Then one should wash the linga and enjoy a suitable woman; this, correctly proclaimed by Nāgārjuna, causes the retention of semen in men. Rmañj_9.2.
A ring made from the tip of a chameleon's tail, wound with threads, should be worn on the little finger; by doing so, a man does not lose his virility.
Having ground lotus seeds with honey, one should smear it upon the navel; as long as this plaster remains, so long will he not emit his semen.
One should take a sparrow's egg and grind it with fresh butter;
by smearing this upon the feet, the stabilization of semen occurs, such that as long as one does not touch the ground, one does not emit semen. Rmañj 9.5.
One should take the tip of the right tusk of a wild boar and bind it above the waist;
thereby, the stiffening of semen occurs.
One should fetch a black-colored snake known by the name Dhuṇḍubha.
A man who wears her bone on his hip does not emit semen;

Having uprooted the root of red Apāmārga on a Tuesday morning after it has been consecrated with mantras on a Monday, and having tied it around one's waist, one does not lose semen.
A pala of khaśa root boiled in water with a sixteenth part of jaggery, drunk at night with sour gruel, prevents the emission of semen during sexual intercourse for men. (Rmañj 9.10)
If one should eat suraṇa root and the root of tulasī together with betel leaf, a man will not lose his virility; there is no doubt that each of these alone achieves this.
One should smear the penis with boar fat together with honey;
the man's penis will then become thick, firm, and long.
The filaments of the white lotus (puṇḍarīka), ground together with honey and applied to the penis,
will undoubtedly cause it to fall away even during sexual intercourse.
If the root of the *lāṅgalī* plant is buried in the place of sexual union under the auspicious constellation of Anurādhā, it will certainly cause the destruction of virility.
If one consumes food and drink prepared with the powder of six *tinduka* fruits, processed overnight and mixed with goat’s urine, it causes impotence in men.
The powder of sesame and gokṣura, cooked with goat’s milk, when consumed cold and mixed with honey, destroys impotence. (Rmañj 9.16)
If one who is barren should smear the spider’s web with honey and smear its center with that, she who is bound in barrenness shall be liberated.
The juice produced from jasmine alone is already a great intoxicant;
how much more so when it is combined with honey, camphor, and mercury?
Fresh ginger, sulphur, black mustard, and borax— these,
ground together in equal proportions, should be cast into lime juice.
Then one should place it on for three *ghaṭikās* or hold it in the hand; as many women as there are, five in number, will indeed smell it and run [to the practitioner]. (Rmañj 9.20)
When the powder made from the leaves and fruits of the *mahāriṣṭa* is mixed with honey and applied as an ointment to the penis, women become aroused during sexual intercourse.
One whose sense organs are smeared with this mixture of honey, rock salt,
and pigeon excrement makes a beautiful woman act like a servant during sexual union.
The lord of monkeys, the moon, saffron, gold, and honey—
when one's senses are anointed with these, one makes a beautiful woman behave like a servant during lovemaking.
Having written the name situated in the center of the square, the fourfold *hrīṃ* on its exterior, and the fourfold *klīṃ* outside of that— all of this upon a stone slab— Rmañj_9.24.
When established in honey during the conjunction of an auspicious lunar mansion, this machine certainly and swiftly attracts a woman; of this there is no doubt.
One should prepare equal parts of sandalwood, tagara, kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu, nāgakeśara, kṛṣṇā, and tintiḍika.
And one should cause [it] to be given for seven days by means of oneself as the fifth;
it should be administered in food and drink to a woman or likewise to a man. (Rmañj 9.27)
One should prepare equal parts of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *madhupuṣpī*, *kuñcikīpattrikā*, and white mountain [ash].
For seven days, one should cause [the substance] to be administered, joined with the impurity of oneself as the fifth;
it should be given in food and drink as a supreme means of subjugation.

Having consecrated it seven times with the previously mentioned mantra, one should then give it. One should take the dust from a donkey produced from its body while it is agitated, as well as the ashes of a corpse combined with the menstrual blood of a woman. (Rmañj 9.30)
Having combined these, one should cast them upon the bed or even the seat at night;
hatred will certainly arise, as stated in the *Mālatīmata*.
I shall now describe another supreme and excellent yoga that causes intense enmity: two dogs, fighting with one another, become mutually antagonistic. (Ramañjuśrī-mūlakalpa 9.32)
Taking the dust from those two, the sexual pleasure of women is destroyed;
it truly becomes hatred—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Rmañj 9.33)
When the vulva is constantly washed with the bark of the *amala* tree,
even an elderly woman experiences sexual pleasure like a young girl.
If the seeds of the *sapadma* plant, mixed with sugar, are consumed with lotus water for one month,
they will cause the pair of breasts of women to become exceedingly firm.
Oil cooked with a decoction of powdered *muṇḍī* and applied will cause the breasts of a woman whose youth has declined to swell once again.
By applying a paste of powdered yellow orpiment with that very same water, the mass of hair falls out instantly; this performs a most wonderful marvel. (Rmañj 9.37)
One should burn palāśa, ciñcā, sesame, māṣa, and conch, along with apāmārga and pippalī;
by applying a paste of the powder of realgar and yellow orpiment, it makes the head hairless in an instant.
Having ground the roots of *taṇḍulīyaka* with rice-water,
if they are drunk for three days at the end of the menstrual period, they render a woman barren.
If a woman grinds a *japā* flower with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) and drinks it for three days during her fertile period, she will become barren. (Rmañj 9.40)
When the vaginal opening has been fumigated with nimba wood in the proper manner at the end of her fertile period,
that woman, when she enjoys union, will be free from the suffering of pregnancy.
Taking dhattūra and mallikā flowers and placing them at the waist certainly prevents pregnancy in women such as widows, prostitutes, and the like.
By consuming the powder of *nāgakeśara* flowers with cow’s ghee during her fertile period, while subsisting on milk and rice, a woman obtains a son. (Rmañj 9.43)
The seeds of the *mātuluṅga* tree, steamed in milk with clarified butter, cause even a barren woman to conceive when taken as a drink. (Rmañj 9.44)
One should grind the seeds of the citron together with a maiden;
this should be administered with milk, and one will undoubtedly obtain a pregnancy.
Pippalī, ginger, black pepper, and likewise saffron should be drunk together with ghee; this is a supreme means for bestowing pregnancy upon a barren woman.
A maiden who grinds the root of the *lakṣmaṇā* plant, which was uprooted during the Puṣya asterism,
and drinks it with ghee and milk at the end of her menstrual period, shall obtain a pregnancy.
I shall now describe another excellent yoga by which she may become fruitful:
uśīra, madhuyaṣṭī, lodhra, and also indrayava.
One should prepare equal parts of ghee, resin of the *sarja* tree, honey, *trāyamāṇaka*, and the roots of the *śobhāñjanaka*.
Having ground that substance, one should then cook it with goat's milk;
a woman should drink it for seven nights, as long as the menstrual blood remains.
Then, once the womb has been purified, one should subsequently administer the great medicine;
it should be given for both nasal inhalation and drinking, combined with the milk of a virgin.
By that means, she obtains a son who is truthful and honored by the gods;
one should administer garlic mixed with milk as both a nasal drop and a drink.
One should administer a powder made from *aśvagandhā* with goat’s milk,
along with *yavakṣāra*, *viḍaṅga*, *guḍūcī*, and *hareṇukā*.
Having made all these into equal portions and prepared them as an excellent powder, that woman who drinks this shall obtain a son; of this there is no doubt.
Asafoetida, śatavīryā, pomegranate, rock salt,
the three pungents, śatapuṣpā, nāgapuṣpa, and śatāvarī.
One should cause madhuka and sumanā to be given in measures of a karṣa;
they should be administered with milk for both women and men.
For three days, she should consume rice grains with milk;
having eaten this, a woman will conceive—of this there is no doubt.
The root of *arka*, *priyaṅgu*, *kusumbha*, *nāgakeśara*, *balā*, and *atibalā*, drunk for three days with goat's milk, [achieves the desired result]. (Rmañj 9.58)
They purify the womb, and thereafter one should administer a great medicine:
blue lotus, *tagara*, costus, liquorice, and sandalwood.
One should have her take these ground with goat's milk for five days;
furthermore, one should give her a drink mixed with *lakṣmaṇā* and cow's milk.
By that means, she obtains a son who is richly endowed with the marks and highly wise;
when the blood has departed and the womb is pure, Lakṣmaṇā likewise becomes full of milk.
When administered as a nasal drop or a drink, a woman obtains a son;
[the herbs used are] white arka, kṣudranī, white śvetā, and white girikarṇikā.
Lakṣmaṇā and vandhyākarkoṭī, combined with cow’s milk, should be administered as a nasal drop or taken by mouth; by doing so, one obtains conception through sexual union.
One may arrest a falling fetus by using potter’s clay;
or by drinking honey with the milk of a she-goat, or alternatively, white *adrikarṇikā*.
Lalanā, sugar, pāṭhā, and kanda, when consumed together with honey,
certainly prevent a fetus situated [in the womb] from falling.
Powdered rice from *śāli* grains mixed with an equal portion of sugar,
when drunk in a decoction of the roots of the *udumbara* tree, well protects the fetus.
The roots of the mātuluṅga plant mixed with madhuka and honey,
to be drunk together with ghee, cause a woman to give birth easily.
A pregnant woman should smear her feet with the root of *lāṅgalī* rubbed with cold water; she will quickly bring about delivery.
For those women who have no onset of menses at the time of their fertile period,
one should perform this treatment so that the onset of menses may occur again.
The physician should prepare a pill from long pepper, alkali of barley, *viḍaṅga*, the fruit of *manmatha*, and the bitter seeds of *tumbinī*. (Rmañj 9.70)
When Muṇḍī is combined with milk and applied to the vaginal opening, a woman becomes auspicious;
within three, five, or seven nights, menstruation occurs, and not otherwise.
I shall now briefly proclaim the Bālatantra as spoken by Rāvaṇa:
the ritual substances, the directions and their divisions, the mantra, and the characteristics of its reception.
On the first day, month, or year, she seizes the child; she is known by the name Mandā, and these are her characteristics. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 9.73)
On the second day, month, or year, she seizes the child;
the yoginī named Sunandā first produces a fever.
Contraction of the hands and feet, eye disease, excessive vomiting, a state of fear, and emaciation—these are the characteristics of one seized by that [demon]. (Rmañj 9.75)
On the third day, month, or year, a female spirit named Pūtanā, a yoginī, seizes the child; there is a breaking pain in the limbs, fever, and loss of appetite.

One should offer the bali-oblation for five nights during the afternoon in the western direction (vāruṇī) to one characterized by incoherent speech, swelling of the neck, vomiting, and other such symptoms.
On the fourth day, month, or year, she seizes the child;
when seized by her, who is named Biḍālī, there is pain in the eyes, fever, and loss of appetite.
With the mantra beginning "gātramāṭenama," one should offer the oblation with discolored [substances];
on the fifth day, month, or year, she seizes the child. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 9.79)
The Yoginī known as Nartakī has these characteristics:
on the sixth day of the month or year, she seizes a child.
The symptoms of the disease named Yoginī-śakunī are cough, dyspnea, loss of appetite, fever, contraction of the hands, feet, and other limbs, and pain in the eyes. (Rmañj 9.81)
For five nights, one should offer a bali-oblation to her in the western direction;
on the seventh day, month, or year, the withered Śivā shall [devour] the child.

If the child seizes [the affliction] characterized by weeping, trembling, fever, emaciation, and so forth, and if one offers the *bali* in the western direction five times, the child becomes happy. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 9.83)
On the eighth day, month, or year, the Jṛmbhakā seizes [the victim];
as soon as one is seized by her, fever first arises.
For those suffering from headaches, eye diseases, or attempts to gouge out the eyes,
one should offer an oblation to her while facing the southern direction.
On the ninth day, month, or year, she seizes the child;
she is named Acintā Yoginī, and her symptoms are the breaking of limbs, pain in the head, and eyeache.
Vomiting, delirium, and so forth are the symptoms of one seized by that [spirit].
One should cause an offering to be presented to it, having taken recourse to the northern direction.
On the tenth day, month, or year, she seizes the child;
she is known by the name Kāpālikā, and these are the characteristics of that Yoginī.
Tearing, trembling, vomiting, fever, weakness, and pain in the eyes [occur];
one should offer an oblation for five nights while resorting to the eastern direction.
On the eleventh day, month, or year, she seizes one who desires her;
trembling of the limbs and intense fever are the symptoms of one possessed by her.
On the day, month, or year numbered by the sun (twelfth), the Yoginī named Pītalī seizes the child; there is weeping, pain, and fever.
One who suffers from sleeplessness, a weakened voice, a yellow complexion, vomiting,
and a lack of appetite should offer a bali-oblation for seven nights while facing the northern direction.
On the day, month, or year numbered by the *kāma* (five), Bhadrakālī seizes the child;
[the fever] named Jvara causes the trembling of the left hand.

One should cause an offering to be presented to her, who has sensations, a fondness for fragrances, and labored breathing; whose body is yellow and whose movements are erratic, by resorting to the eastern direction.
In the month of Purandara-dina, during the year, she seizes the child;
for she is the Yoginī named Tārā, [causing] fever, wasting, and intense loss of appetite.
If there is a sign of eye affliction, one should offer a bali-oblation to her on the fifteenth day, at the end of a fortnight, a month, or a year; she seizes the child.

The Yoginī named Śarvarī causes asthma, cough, loss of appetite, and fever; when one is seized by her, these are the signs, and so forth—one should cast an offering in the southern direction. (Rmañj 9.97)
On the day of transformation, in the month, or in the year, the Yoginī seizes [the victim];
the maiden experiences distress of the eyes and symptoms such as fever and emaciation.

Taking recourse in the southwestern direction (nairṛtī), one who knows the mantras should offer the bali-oblation for seven nights; thereafter, he should bathe the child with water consecrated by the rite of pacification (śānti).
Having fashioned the form of the Goddess from earth drawn from both banks of a river,
worship should be performed with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings by the king.
Sweets, cakes, and pastries; choice food, molasses, and curd;
banners representing the four castes; radiant lamps, flowers, and sandalwood.
One should worship [the deities] for all diseases in the afternoon with offerings according to the ritual manual;
in every case, the offering of the *bali* is performed under a distinct name.
Now, O Mañjuśrī, I shall explain the knowledge of time as it truly is,
by which a yogi comes to know life and death with certainty. (Mañj 10.1)
He between whose two fangs the world is held like a morsel in a mouth—
whether today or at dawn— he will certainly come to pass.
Having understood the taste, the elixir, the application, and the time, one should practice;
since it is useless without knowledge, that [knowledge] is now being explained.

A messenger wearing red, dyed, or black garments, an elephant-tusked man afflicted by old age, his body and weapons smeared with oil, his face filled with dejected tears, carrying ashes, charcoal, a skull-bowl, dust, and a pestle— whoever stands facing the sun at sunrise or sunset— such a person shall serve as the executioner for those who are diseased.
Sudden change of mind, sudden [appearance of] a supreme person,
and sudden arising of the sense faculties— these are the characteristics of a *sannipāta* (aggregation of humors).
In one whose body has become cold, there occurs a transformation of the natural state;
understand from me that in such a case, death-signs (ariṣṭa) pervade it in brief.
One who delights in harsh words and becomes angry at kind words,
and who suddenly stops listening— such a person should be declared to have reached the end of his life.
Or the person who does not perceive a fragrance when the lamp has gone out, and who likewise sees the luminaries blazing by day; Rmañj_10.8 //
One may see the moon possessing the radiance of the sun, or the sun with the splendor of the moon;
or one may see clouds nourished by lightning and wind, moving through the stainless sky.
He sees the sky crowded with celestial palaces, vehicles,
and mansions, and he beholds the atmosphere as a dark blue, embodied form.
He who perceives heat as if it were cold, and cold as if it were heat—
he in whom such doubt has arisen, they say, is one whose life has come to an end.
The man who perceives other entities through a distorted lens is like one seeing the earth shrouded by smoke, mist, or clouds. (Ramañjari 10.12)
He who perceives the eighteenfold earth with its boundary lines as if the world were ablaze or as if it were submerged in water; (Rm 10.13)
For he who does not see his own reflection in the waters as in a mirror of moonlight, or sees it with a missing limb, or perceives it as deformed; // Rmñj_10.14 //
That man who has departed for the realm of dogs, crows, kaṅkas, vultures, yakṣas,
rākṣasas, piśācas, uragas, and nāgas, even though it is a place of deformity—
He whose modesty and splendor perish, as well as his vigor, vitality, and memory,
and who yawns unexpectedly— he is undoubtedly one whose life-force has departed.
He whose lower lip falls away while the upper remains fixed, or conversely,
he for whom there is a fear regarding the noose— his life is difficult to preserve.
If one's nose is crooked, cracked, or even numb,
or if it quivers or sinks down, that person is undoubtedly deprived of life.
When one does not see one's own reflection in the eyes of others,
and when one's vision becomes blurred, then death is near at hand.
When the self perceives itself in any way as being deprived of its ears,
it has been swallowed by Time and does not live in this world.
For one who experiences burning at night and coldness by day, with the throat filled with phlegm, death will surely occur; of this there is no doubt.
If one's feet are cold, the region of the navel is cold, and yet there is heat in the head, death will surely come; of this there is no doubt.
He whose *huṃ* sound is cool, yet whose *phuṭ* sound resembles fire, and who is constantly burning—for him there is death, without a doubt. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 10.23)
Those whose weapons have failed them do not see Arundhatī, nor Dhruva, nor the three steps of Viṣṇu; they do not even see the fourth, the circle of the Mothers.
Having seen the disk of the sun without its rays, or fire devoid of its flames,
a person does not live beyond eleven months.
He who [sees] wind, urine, feces, gold,
or silver either directly or in a dream does not live for ten months.
If a man sees a forest shining like gold in some place,
or sees deformed beings, he will not live for nine months.
Even one with a large body may suddenly become thin, or one who is thin may suddenly assume bulkiness; one who is dark may become golden-hued, or even one who is fair may take on a black complexion.

A man who is steadfast, skilled in wealth and dharma through his fortitude, and peaceful yet helpful—if such a person experiences a sudden change in his natural state during the eighth month, it portends death.

If there be pain in the palm of the hand, at the root of the tongue, and if the blood is dark at its source, that man will not see any prosperity whatsoever; indeed, such a person shall live for only seven months.
He whose three middle fingers wither away without illness, whose throat dries up, who suffers from frequent discharge and numbness, passes away in the sixth month. (Rmañj 10.30)
He for whom there is no movement whatsoever regarding his actions will certainly, in the fifth month, depart mounted upon the [five] aggregates.
If the light does not flash forth when both eyes are pressed,
his death is declared to be certain in the fourth month.
He whose testicles throb even when not afflicted by anything at all will certainly go to the world of Yama in the third month.

O Tārā, if one sees the moon’s radiance during the day, or lightning in a chasm at the end of night, or a rainbow by oneself at night, they say that his death will occur within two months. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 10.34)
If there is no movement whatsoever from the vital point located at the knee, his death will occur at the end of a month; it cannot be delayed by anyone.
When the middle joint of the little finger is black,
it is said that the life of men has reached its end within a limit of eighteen days.
He who sees himself without a head in ghee, oil, water, or even in a mirror,
lives for only one fortnight.
For one for whom coldness, curd, rice, and drinks become causes of heat,
there shall be cool rays, a beautiful smile, and then perfect purity.
That man who does not perceive what is pleasant nor perceive heat lives for only one fortnight,
as declared by the knowledge of time.
If these three— the heart, the hands, and the feet— dry up at that very moment for one who has just bathed, he shall live for ten nights.
He who does not see the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, the eyes, or the joining of the lips— things previously seen— for seven nights, he lives.
If one's stream [of breath] falls upon the ground as drops, death will occur within seven days; this is declared by the knowledge of time.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the shadow-person (chāyāpuruṣa),
by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes a knower of the three times.
That means by which even this time situated at a distance is perceived,
they describe in brief according to what is taught in the Śiva-āgama.
Having gone to a solitary, secluded place and placing the sun behind one's back,
one should gaze intently at one's own shadow as it falls upon the region of the throat.
Then one should gaze at the sky; then one sees Śaṅkara.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, that which is auspicious is indeed seen.
Resembling pure crystal, Hara assumes various forms;
through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes the lord of those who roam the earth.
O Lord, within two years, that yogi—himself the master who is both creator and destroyer—attains knowledge of the three times; of this there is no doubt. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 10.48)
Through the yoga of practiced cultivation, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to attain;
one beholds that form, black in color, within the stainless sky.
That yogin will meet death within six months; there is no doubt about this.
Yellow indicates fear of disease, while red and blue indicate murder. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 10.50)
Great distress arises regarding this body of manifold colors;
the feet, the ankles, and the belly become emaciated by destruction. (Ramañjari 10.51)
Whether within half a year, a year, or not even two years,
if [the mark] on the right arm disappears, one's own kinsman will certainly die.
Likewise, on the left arm, the wife perishes—of this there is no doubt;
on the head and both right arms, one should predict destruction and death.
Without the head, death occurs within a month; without the calves, in nine days;
with the destruction of the shoulders, in eight days; and by the disappearance of the shadow, at that very moment.
Through bathing at sacred fords, through giving, through austerity, or through virtuous deeds;
through recitation, or through the yoga of knowledge—the bondage of time is produced.
The previously mentioned elixir (*rasāyana*) and the pill that restores life to the dead should be used by men as prescribed; it is the supreme binding of time.
Therefore, the body must be protected, since it is the means for accomplishing dharma and other goals;
these defects, which reside in the bodily constituents and impurities, destroy the physical frame.
The *Rasamañjarī* was composed by the wise Śālinātha, son of Vaidyanātha, after he had examined and extracted [the essence] from the treatises.
